pages.title: Getting started
pages.summary: From the demo or your first sign-in to adding, scheduling and completing your first task, in about five minutes.
pages.html:
Getting started

This guide takes you from opening OpenTodo for the first time to adding a task, giving it a date and ticking it off. It takes about five minutes. You can follow along in the demo or on your own server.

Open OpenTodo#

You have three ways in.

Try the demo#

Go to demo.open-todo.app and select Try the demo. You get a private sandbox filled with sample projects and tasks. Nobody else can see it, and it is deleted after two hours without activity (and every night), so don't keep anything personal there.

Set up your own server#

The first person to open a new OpenTodo server creates the owner account. Enter your name, email and a password of at least 10 characters, then select Create owner account. After that, sign-up is closed: other people join with an invitation from you (see Sharing and comments).

Join with an invitation#

Open the invitation link you were sent, choose a name and password, and you're in. If your server offers single sign-on or passkeys, the sign-in screen shows those buttons too.

Once you're signed in, the app is stored on your device. You can keep using it without a connection, and it catches up with the server when you're back online.

Find your way around#

The sidebar on the left lists your views and projects. On a phone it's behind the menu button at the top left.

  • Inbox collects tasks that don't belong to a project yet.
  • Today shows what's due today, with anything overdue at the top.
  • Upcoming shows the days ahead, grouped by date.
  • Projects are your own lists, like "Home renovation" or "Work".

The circle to the left of each task completes it. The small line under the title shows the date, labels and project. More on all the views in Views.

Add your first task#

  1. Press q, or click the Add a task box at the top of the list.
  2. Type what you need to do, for example Call the dentist.
  3. Press Enter.

The task appears straight away. The box stays open, so you can type the next one right after.

Where the task goes depends on where you are: in a project it goes into that project, in Today it's due today, and in the Inbox it waits there until you sort it.

Give it a date#

You can schedule a task while you type it. Quick add understands everyday words:

Call the dentist tomorrow at 9am

As you type, small chips appear under the box to show what OpenTodo understood: a date chip for "tomorrow at 9am", and below them the title that will be saved. If a word was picked up by mistake ("May" as in the name, not the month), click the × on its chip and it stays part of the title.

The same line can also set a project with #, a label with @, a priority from p1 (highest) to p4, and how long it will take with +, like +15m. The quick add reference lists everything it understands, in six languages.

To change the date later, open the task (click it, or select it and press Enter) and use Due in the panel that opens.

Complete it#

When you're done, click the circle next to the task, or select it with j and k and press c. The task leaves the list and moves to Completed in the sidebar. Changed your mind? Open Completed and reopen it.

Get it on your phone#

OpenTodo runs in the browser, and you can install it like an app on your phone, tablet or computer. It then opens in its own window and works offline. See Installing the app.

Help inside the app#

Every guide on this site is also in the app: select Help at the bottom of the sidebar, or press g then ?. It works offline and matches the version of your server. Many screens have a small Help link that opens the right section next to what you're doing, without closing it.

Where to go next#

  • Tasks and projects: notes, subtasks, priorities and organising your work.
  • Views: Today, Upcoming, the calendar and views you save yourself.
  • Recurring tasks and reminders: repeat a task every week and get a nudge on time.
  • Keyboard shortcuts: press ? in the app to see them all.

pages.title: Installing the app
pages.summary: Put OpenTodo on your home screen or desktop so it opens in its own window and works offline, on iPhone, Android, Windows, macOS and Linux.
pages.html:
Installing the app

OpenTodo is a web app you can install. Once installed it has its own icon, opens in its own window without browser bars, starts without a connection, and on most platforms can show reminders while it's closed. There is no app store involved: you install it from your server's address, and updates arrive by themselves.

Before you start, open your OpenTodo address in the browser and sign in once. Installing needs a secure address (one starting with https://); if your browser offers no install option at all, ask whoever runs your server to set that up.

iPhone and iPad#

  1. Open your OpenTodo address in Safari.
  2. Tap the Share button (the square with an arrow pointing up).
  3. Scroll down and tap Add to Home Screen, then Add.

OpenTodo now has an icon on your home screen. Open it from there from now on. On iOS 16.4 and later, push notifications for reminders work only in the installed app, not in a Safari tab; turn them on in Settings → Notifications inside the app. See Notifications.

Recent iOS versions also offer Add to Home Screen from the share menu of other browsers. If you don't see it, use Safari.

Android#

  1. Open your OpenTodo address in Chrome (Edge and Samsung Internet work the same way).
  2. Open the browser menu (⋮).
  3. Tap Install app. On some versions it's called Add to Home screen.

Chrome sometimes shows an install banner at the bottom of the screen on its own; tapping it does the same thing.

After installing, OpenTodo also appears in Android's share menu, so you can send a link or some text from another app straight into a new task. See Capturing pages.

Windows, macOS, Linux and ChromeOS#

In Chrome or Edge:

  1. Open your OpenTodo address.
  2. Click the install icon at the right end of the address bar (a small screen with a down arrow), or open the browser menu and choose Install OpenTodo (in Edge: Apps → Install this site as an app).
  3. Confirm with Install.

OpenTodo opens in its own window and gets an entry in your Start menu, Dock or app launcher. You can pin it to the taskbar like any other app.

In Safari on macOS (Sonoma or later), choose File → Add to Dock.

Firefox on the desktop doesn't install web apps. You can still use OpenTodo in a Firefox tab with everything working, including offline use once the page has loaded.

Keep using it offline#

The installed app keeps a full copy of your tasks on the device. You can open it on a plane, add and complete tasks, and it syncs when you're online again. The status at the top right tells you where things stand. More in Offline and sync.

Updates#

When your server is updated, the app fetches the new version in the background and switches to it on its own, usually with one quick reload. If you think you're still on an old version, close the app completely and open it again.

Remove it#

Remove it the way you remove any app on that device: long-press the icon and choose Remove App (iPhone) or Uninstall (Android), or use Uninstall from the app window's menu on a computer. Your tasks stay on your server.

Signing out (Settings → Account → Sign out of this device) clears the copy of your tasks on that device. Changes that haven't reached the server yet are uploaded first when you're online.

pages.title: Switch from Todoist
pages.summary: Move your Todoist projects, sections, subtasks, labels, priorities and dates to OpenTodo in a few minutes.
pages.html:
Switch from Todoist

Your projects, sections, subtasks, labels, priorities, due dates and recurring tasks come with you. It takes a few minutes, and you can undo the whole import with one click.

Export from Todoist#

Use a backup: it holds every project and keeps their names.

  1. In Todoist, open its settings and find Backups.
  2. Download the latest backup. It is a ZIP file such as Todoist_backup_2026-09-19.zip.

A single project can also be exported as CSV from the project's menu, but a lone CSV file does not say which project it was, so its tasks go to the project you choose when importing.

Import into OpenTodo#

  1. Open Settings → Data → Import data (or press g then Shift+I).
  2. Choose the ZIP file. The preview shows Todoist backup (ZIP) and lists every project, section and task.
  3. Check the warnings, choose a time zone if your tasks have times, and select Import.

Projects that were boards in Todoist open as boards on this device. Your other devices receive everything on their next sync.

What carries over#

  • Projects, sections and subtasks (by their indent), in the same order.
  • Priorities: Todoist's red flag is p1, as you saw it.
  • Labels written in tasks (@errands), removed from the title.
  • Descriptions and estimates (task durations in minutes).
  • Due dates and times, in the language you used Todoist in (English, German, French, Italian, Spanish or Portuguese). Dates without a year take the year of the backup.
  • Recurring dates such as every monday or jeden Montag, when OpenTodo's recurrence rules can express them.
  • Reminders with a time or an offset.

The full mapping is in Import formats.

What does not#

  • Comments are added to the task's description under "Comments", because their authors cannot be kept.
  • Deadlines are kept as a "Deadline: …" line in the description; OpenTodo has no deadline field yet.
  • Assignees are dropped; invite people and share the project instead.
  • Dates or rules OpenTodo cannot read leave the task without a due date, with a warning that quotes them.

Changed your mind? Undo the import from the list of past imports.

pages.title: Switch from Things
pages.summary: Bring your Things 3 areas, projects, headings, to-dos, checklists and tags to OpenTodo by copying its database.
pages.html:
Switch from Things

Things 3 has no export button, but OpenTodo can read a copy of its database directly. Your areas, projects, headings, to-dos, checklists, tags and notes come with you.

Copy the Things database#

On a Mac, as Cultured Code's support article "Accessing the Things database" describes:

  1. Quit Things. The copy must be made while the app is closed.
  2. In Finder, choose Go → Go to Folder and open ~/Library/Group Containers/JLMPQHK86H.com.culturedcode.ThingsMac/.
  3. Open the ThingsData-… folder and copy (do not move) Things Database.thingsdatabase to your Desktop.
  4. Right-click the copy, choose Show Package Contents, and find main.sqlite. Alternatively, compress the whole folder into a ZIP.

On iPhone or iPad, the same article lists a diagnostics code (Settings → General → Diagnostics → Enter Code) that sends Things Database.aar. Save it to Files, tap it to unpack it into Things Database.thingsdatabase, and use the main.sqlite inside.

Import into OpenTodo#

  1. Open Settings → Data → Import data (or press g then Shift+I).
  2. Choose main.sqlite (or the ZIP). The preview shows Things 3 database.
  3. Check the warnings and select Import.

The file is read on your server from a private copy, read-only, and deleted right after the preview or import.

What carries over#

  • Areas become parent projects; projects stay inside them.
  • Headings become sections; to-dos keep their heading.
  • Checklist items become subtasks, completed ones included.
  • Tags become labels (nested tags as parent/child).
  • Notes, the start date ("When") as the due date, and reminder times.
  • Repeating to-dos, when OpenTodo's recurrence rules can express them.
  • Completed and canceled items (canceled ones get the label canceled).

The full mapping is in Import formats.

What does not#

  • Deadlines are kept as a "Deadline: …" line in the description.
  • Someday and This Evening are not imported as such; the to-dos arrive with a warning.
  • Trashed items are skipped.

pages.title: Switch from TickTick
pages.summary: Move your TickTick folders, lists, columns, checklists, tags, priorities, dates and reminders to OpenTodo.
pages.html:
Switch from TickTick

Your folders, lists, board columns, checklists, tags, priorities, due dates, reminders and repeating tasks come with you.

Export from TickTick#

TickTick creates a backup as one CSV file from its settings (look for Backup). Download it; it is named like TickTick-backup-2026-10-14.csv.

Import into OpenTodo#

  1. Open Settings → Data → Import data (or press g then Shift+I).
  2. Choose the CSV file. The preview shows TickTick backup (CSV).
  3. Check the warnings and select Import.

Lists you used as a board (kanban) open as boards on this device.

What carries over#

  • Folders become parent projects; lists become projects inside them.
  • Board columns become sections.
  • Checklists become a task with one subtask per item; checked items are completed.
  • Subtasks, tags, descriptions and priorities (high, medium, low, none become p1–p4).
  • Due dates and times as you saw them, all-day tasks as dates.
  • Reminders and repeat rules, when OpenTodo's recurrence rules can express them.
  • Completed tasks; abandoned ones are completed with the label canceled.

The full mapping is in Import formats.

What does not#

  • Attachments, habits, focus records and comments are not part of the CSV backup.
  • Repeat rules OpenTodo cannot express are dropped with a warning; the task is kept.

pages.title: Switch from Linear
pages.summary: Bring your Linear issues to OpenTodo with their projects, statuses as board columns, priorities, labels and sub-issues.
pages.html:
Switch from Linear

OpenTodo is a good fit for small teams and personal work that want speed without process. Your issues come with their projects, statuses, priorities, labels, due dates and sub-issues.

Export from Linear#

Linear exports a workspace's issues as one CSV file from its workspace settings (look for Import / Export).

Import into OpenTodo#

  1. Open Settings → Data → Import data (or press g then Shift+I).
  2. Choose the CSV file. The preview shows Linear export (CSV).
  3. Check the warnings and select Import.

Each project opens as a board on this device, with one column per status.

What carries over#

  • Projects (or teams, for issues without a project).
  • Statuses become sections, in the order they appear, so the board shows the same columns.
  • Titles, and descriptions that start with the issue identifier (ENG-123), so you can still find it.
  • Priorities (Urgent, High, Medium, Low and No priority become p1–p4), labels and due dates.
  • Sub-issues as subtasks.
  • Completed issues; canceled ones are completed with the label canceled.
  • Issues assigned to you stay assigned to you.

The full mapping is in Import formats.

What does not#

  • Blocked by relations between issues in the export become Blocked by on the tasks. Estimates (points), cycles, milestones, initiatives, SLAs and the other issue relations (related, duplicate) are dropped with a warning.
  • Issues assigned to other people arrive unassigned; share the project and assign them again.
  • Comments and attachments are not part of the CSV export.

pages.title: Tasks and projects
pages.summary: Add and edit tasks, write notes, break work into subtasks, set priorities and organise everything into projects and sub-projects.
pages.html:
Tasks and projects

A task is one thing to do. A project is a list of tasks that belong together. This guide covers both, from adding a task to arranging projects inside each other.

Add a task#

Press q anywhere in a task list, type, and press Enter. The box stays focused so you can add several in a row.

You can fill in details as you type:

Order new taps friday #Home @errand p2 +20m

This creates "Order new taps", due Friday, in the project Home, with the label errand, priority 2 and an estimate of 20 minutes. Chips under the box show what was understood before you press Enter. The quick add reference has every word and symbol it knows.

New tasks without a project land in the Inbox. Tasks added inside a project go into that project, and tasks added in Today are due today.

Edit a task#

Click a task, or select it with j / k and press Enter, to open its panel. Every change is saved as you make it; there is no Save button.

The top of the panel has Complete, a ⋯ menu with Copy link, Open parent task, Open recurring task and Delete, and the × that closes it. Below are the Title and Notes. Notes can have headings, bold and italic text, links, and bullet, numbered and check lists.

Then comes the properties card. Each row shows its current value, or a quiet "No due date", "No estimate" and so on when it is empty. Click a row, or Tab to it and press Enter, to change it; Esc closes the editor and leaves you on the row.

  • Project, Section and Parent task move the task. Each opens a list you can search: the projects and tasks you pick most often come first, and nested projects show their path ("Work › Clients"), so two projects with the same name are told apart. Type a new name in Project and choose Create to make a project and move the task into it. A subtask always shows its parent's section.
  • Assignee. See Assign tasks.
  • Priority, from P1 (most important) to P4 (the default). Click one, or press 1 to 4 anywhere in the panel outside a text field.
  • Due, a date with an optional time, and the time zone chip next to it.
  • When (Anytime, a start date or Someday) and Evening. See When a task starts.
  • Deadline, the day the task must be finished by, with how many days are left. Type it like a due date (fri, 2026-11-06) or clear it with ×. See Deadlines.
  • Reminders show as chips. Add reminder offers the usual times before the due time, times before the deadline once the task has one, a custom offset or a set date and time; each chip's ⋯ menu edits, snoozes, dismisses or deletes it.
  • Estimate and Repeat. See Recurring tasks and reminders and Time blocking.
  • Labels: open the row to add, create or remove labels.

Below the card are the Subtasks and the Comments, Activity and History tabs.

If you are a viewer of a shared project, the values read as text and can't be changed, and Complete and Delete are hidden. You can still comment.

Close the panel with Esc or the × at the top. On a phone the panel covers the list; close it to go back.

Quick changes from the list#

You don't have to open a task to change it. Select it and press:

Key Does
1 to 4 Set the priority
c Complete or reopen
L Add labels (type to search, Enter to add or create)
e Set the estimate (20, 45m, 1h30)
d Set the deadline (fri, 2026-11-06)
n Park in Someday, or bring back
Shift+N Defer: type the start date
Shift+E Toggle This Evening
x Tick for a bulk action (see Change several tasks at once)
s Schedule it on the Day calendar
Delete Move it to the Trash

Write notes#

The notes field formats as you type. Start a line with - for a bullet list, 1. for a numbered list, [ ] for a checklist or # for a heading. Select text and press Ctrl+B for bold or Ctrl+K for a link (⌘ on a Mac). If two of your devices edit the same note at the same time, both sets of changes are kept.

Dates and times#

A due date is just a calendar day, and a time is the time on the clock where you are. A task due Tuesday at 09:00 shows Tuesday at 09:00 on every device, even when you travel.

Type the date and time in the Due fields, or pick them. Dates and times are shown in the format you chose in Settings → Preferences → Date and time, and you can type them the same way:

  • Date: a date in your format (14/10 or 10/14, with or without a year), an ISO date (2026-10-14), or a word: today, tomorrow, a weekday such as fri, next week or 3 Nov. A date without a year that has already passed this year means next year. Press Enter or leave the field to save it. If the date doesn't exist (31/02), the field says so and the task keeps its date.
  • Calendar: the calendar button next to the date, or Alt+↓ in the field, opens a month whose weeks start on your first day of the week. Arrow keys move by day and week, Page Up and Page Down by month, Home and End to the start and end of the week, Enter picks the day and Esc closes it.
  • Time: 15, 1530, 15:30, 3pm, 3:30 pm or noon, whichever clock you use. ↓ in the field shows times in 15-minute steps to pick from.

Clear the date to remove the due date, or clear the time to keep only the day.

Under the due date, the time zone button shows how the time is meant: Floating (the same clock time wherever you are) or a city and its offset, such as New York · UTC−5 (one moment worldwide). Choose it to:

  • Fix to my zone: tie the time to your current time zone, for things that happen at a fixed moment. Press z with the panel open to do the same, and again to release it.
  • Fix to another time zone: search any city or zone, for example a call at 15:00 in New York. The panel shows how that reads for you ("15:00 in New York = 21:00 your time (Berlin)") before you choose Fix to New York. Your own zone is listed first, then the zones you used recently.
  • Make floating: release a fixed time to the clock time you currently see.

Devices elsewhere show a fixed time converted to their local time, with the original time and city as a hint. Without a time the button is off: a due date alone always stays floating.

Deadlines#

The due date is when you plan to work on a task. A deadline is the day it must be finished by, and the two are separate: you can plan a report for Tuesday that is due to your boss on Friday. Moving or clearing the due date never changes the deadline, and you may even plan a task after its deadline; the countdown then turns red.

A task with a deadline shows a countdown on its row, next to an hourglass: 3d for three days to go, Today on the day, and 2d over once it has passed. It turns amber in the last week and red on the day and after. Hover it to see the full date. The countdown follows the calendar on your device, so it moves on at midnight even offline.

Deadlines also bring tasks into Today and Upcoming, and you can add a reminder before the deadline (see Reminders).

When a task starts#

Not every task is for now. The When row in the panel says when a task becomes relevant:

  • Anytime, the default: the task is in your lists as usual.
  • A start date defers the task until that day: it disappears from Today, Upcoming, Anytime and the counts, and its project or Inbox lists it at the end under Later, with a Starts 21 Oct chip. On its start day it appears in Today with a Started chip and stays there until you deal with it. The start date can't be after the due date.
  • Someday parks the task: it moves to the Someday view and its project's Later group, and its due date is cleared (a repeating task stops repeating). Giving it a due date or a start date brings it back.

A due date or a deadline that has come always shows the task in Today, even if it is deferred or parked.

This Evening (the Evening switch next to it) moves a task due today into its own group below the day's tasks in Today, and shows a moon on its row elsewhere. It says nothing about the time of day.

From the list: n parks a task or brings it back, Shift+N asks for its start date, and Shift+E toggles This Evening.

Wait for another task#

Some tasks can't start until another is done: you can't book flights before the dates are confirmed. Open the task, choose Blocked by (or select it in a list and press b) and pick the tasks it waits for. The list offers open tasks you can link: the task itself, tasks that already wait for it and tasks shared differently are left out, so you can't make two tasks wait for each other.

While at least one of those tasks is open, the task is blocked: its row is dimmed and shows a lock with the number it's waiting for, on boards too, and in Today it moves to a folded Blocked group at the end. As soon as the last one is completed (or deleted), the task is ready again, on every device. You can still open, edit and complete a blocked task; completing it doesn't touch the tasks it waited for. A repeating task keeps blocking until its series ends, and Blocked by says "repeats" next to it.

Blocks in the panel lists the open tasks waiting for this one; select one to open it. In a shared project, blockers are tasks of the same project, and the person a blocked task is assigned to gets a notification when it's ready to start. Filter for blocked or unblocked to list them (see Labels and filters).

Change several tasks at once#

Tick tasks, then act on all of them in one go.

  • Keyboard: press x (or Space) to tick the selected task, Shift+↓ or Shift+↑ to extend the range, and Ctrl+A (⌘+A) to tick the whole list once something is ticked. Esc clears the ticks (after closing the panel).
  • Mouse: a checkbox appears on each row when you point at it; Shift+click ticks a range, Ctrl/⌘+click ticks one task without opening it.
  • Touch: tap Select above the list to show every checkbox, and Done when you are finished.

While tasks are ticked, a bar above the list says how many and offers Actions (or press .): complete or reopen, priority, labels (added to all, or removed from all), a date (today, tomorrow, next week, none, or one you pick), move to a project or section, assign, and move to the Trash. The usual keys work on the whole selection too: c, 1 to 4, L, Shift+A and Delete. With nothing ticked, . opens the same menu for the selected task. It works in projects, the Inbox, Today, Upcoming, the Filter view and saved views, also offline.

Moving and assigning show the changes first, task by task, because they can change who sees a task or notify someone: Enter applies the checked ones, Esc changes nothing. Everything else applies at once, and a notice with Undo stays for ten seconds (Ctrl/⌘+Z works too). Undo puts every task back in one step, except a task someone changed again since, which keeps the newer value and is named.

Complete, reopen and delete#

Click the circle next to a task, or press c. Completed tasks move to Completed in the sidebar, where you can reopen them.

Deleting a task (the Delete button in the panel, or Delete in the list) moves it to the Trash, along with its subtasks. You can restore it from there. See Trash and history.

Break a task into subtasks#

Big tasks are easier as a few small steps. To add one:

  • open the task and type in Add subtask, or
  • select the task in the list and press a.

Subtasks appear indented under their parent, and the parent shows your progress, like 1/3. You can nest subtasks inside subtasks.

To turn an existing task into a subtask, select it and press Tab: it moves under the task above it. Shift+Tab moves it back out. You can also pick a Parent task in the panel. Use ← and → to fold and unfold a parent's subtasks.

Completing a parent completes all its open subtasks too. When you tick off the last open subtask, OpenTodo asks whether to complete the parent as well; press Enter for yes.

Organise with projects#

Projects keep related tasks together. To create one, click + next to Projects in the sidebar, type a name and choose Create. Pick a parent project in the same form to make it a sub-project.

The Project menu at the top right of a project lets you:

  • pick a colour from the swatches at the top,
  • Move to… another project, or back to the top level. Type to find the target: each candidate shows the projects it sits in, and the project itself and its sub-projects are never offered. m opens the menu straight at this step, and Esc goes back to the menu.
  • Rename it,
  • Archive… it, which hides it and its sub-projects from the sidebar while keeping every task,
  • Delete project…, which moves it to the Trash.

Archive and delete ask first and say what they affect, for example how many open tasks and sub-projects move with the project.

The number next to each project in the sidebar counts its open tasks. When a project with sub-projects is folded, the number includes them.

Inside a project you can also group tasks into sections and show them as a board. That has its own guide: Sections and boards.

Sub-projects#

Sub-projects work like folders: "Work" can hold "Q4 launch", which can hold more. A project's page lists its sub-projects at the bottom with their task counts. Use the small arrow next to a project in the sidebar, or ← / →, to fold and unfold it. Folding is remembered on each device separately.

When a project is done#

When you complete the last open task of a project, OpenTodo offers to archive it; press Enter to accept or any other key to keep it. Projects that have had no open tasks for 30 days are archived automatically, with a notice you can undo. You can turn that off in Settings → Projects (each device has its own setting). To bring an archived project back, open Settings → Projects and select Restore next to it under Archived projects; see Trash and history.

Put things in order#

In the Inbox and in projects, you decide the order. Drag a task to a new place (on a touch screen, press and hold first), or select it and press Alt+↑ / Alt+↓. Alt+Shift+↑ sends it to the top. Dropping a task on the middle of another one makes it a subtask. Projects in the sidebar can be reordered the same way.

Today, Upcoming, labels and filters sort themselves by date and priority, so dragging is switched off there.

Tips#

  • Keep the Inbox as a landing spot: capture fast, then sort into projects once a day.
  • Use priorities sparingly. If everything is P1, nothing is.
  • A task with an estimate shows it on the row, like 30m, which makes it easy to spot quick wins. The Quick wins button above most lists shows only tasks of 15 minutes or less.

pages.title: Views
pages.summary: Inbox, Today, Upcoming, Assigned to me, Completed and the calendar, plus views you save yourself, dashboards and the view each device opens on.

toc.text: Anytime, for when you have time

pages.html:
Views

A view is a way of looking at your tasks. OpenTodo comes with a handful, and you can save your own. Every view is built from the copy of your tasks on your device, so they all work offline and update the moment something changes.

The built-in views#

They're at the top of the sidebar. Each has a shortcut: press g, then the letter.

View Shows Shortcut
Inbox Tasks that aren't in a project yet g i
Today Tasks due today and tasks whose deadline is today, with overdue ones first g t
Upcoming Tasks due after today, and undated tasks with a deadline ahead, grouped by day g u
Anytime Open tasks with no date and no start: things to do whenever there is time g n
Someday Tasks you parked for later, by project g o
Assigned to me Open tasks assigned to you, across projects g a
Day and Week Your timed tasks on a calendar g d, g w
Completed What you finished most recently g c
Filter Any search you can describe g f
Trash Deleted tasks and projects g x
Activity What changed in your shared projects g h

The numbers next to the names count open tasks. Deferred and parked tasks (see When a task starts) are not counted.

Plan your day with Today#

Today is where most people start. Overdue tasks sit in their own group at the top, in red, so nothing slips. Below them are today's tasks, sorted by time.

A deadline brings a task into Today too: a task whose deadline is today shows up even if it has no due date or is planned for later. If the deadline has already passed and the task isn't planned for today, it sits under Overdue. Each task is listed once, and the Today count in the sidebar counts the same tasks.

A task whose start date has come shows up in Today too, with a Started chip, and stays until you complete it, give it a date or defer it again. Deferred and parked tasks stay out of Today, unless their due date or deadline has come: a hard date always wins. Tasks you marked for This Evening are listed in their own group below the day's tasks.

Tasks waiting for another task gather in a Blocked group at the end, folded so they don't crowd the day; select the heading to open it (your choice is kept on this device). When the task they wait for is completed, they move up among today's tasks by themselves. In Upcoming and other lists, blocked tasks stay in place, dimmed, with a lock.

Anything you add here with quick add is due today, unless you type another date. To push a task to later, open it and change Due, or press s to place it on the Day calendar.

Plan your week with Upcoming#

Upcoming lists everything that has a date after today, under headings like Tomorrow and the weekday names. It's a good place for a short weekly review: scan the next few days, move what won't fit, and spot empty days.

A task with a deadline but no due date is listed under its deadline day, after the tasks due that day, so you see it while there is still time to plan it. A task with both dates is listed under its due date only; its row shows the deadline countdown. Deferred and parked tasks are left out until they start.

Anytime, for when you have time#

Anytime lists every open task that has no due date, no deadline and no start date, grouped by project: the things you could do whenever there is a moment. A task leaves it as soon as it gets a date, from any device.

Park ideas in Someday#

Someday holds the tasks you parked: ideas and maybes you don't want to see every day. They stay out of Today, Upcoming, Anytime and the counts, and are listed here by project and in their project's Later group. Anything you add in this view is parked. Press n on a task to park it or bring it back.

When you want to see the hours, switch to Week, which shows your timed tasks as blocks on a grid. See Time blocking.

Narrow a list by duration#

Above most lists are four buttons: Quick wins (15 minutes or less), Under 30 min, Over 1 h and Unestimated. Turn one on to see only matching tasks; select it again to clear it. Your choice is remembered on that device. Estimates are set with e or in the task panel.

Save your own views#

When the built-in views aren't enough, describe what you want in the Filter view, then save it. For example, blocked lists every task waiting for another one (save it as Waiting for), @waiting & open lists everything you labelled as waiting, and due <= 7 days & p1 shows urgent tasks for the coming week. The filter language is explained in Labels and filters.

To save the current filter, press s in the results (or use the save button), and give it a name. Saved views are pinned to the Views group in the sidebar with a live count, and they sync to all your devices.

Each saved view can group its tasks (by project, date, priority or label) and sort them (by date, priority, your own order, creation time or title). Change these from the top of the view. To change the query itself, press /, edit it and press Enter.

The All link next to Views (or g v) opens the list of all your saved views. From there you can rename, reorder, unpin or delete them.

Every saved view has the same menu, wherever you open it: the ⋯ button on its row in the sidebar or the views list, its header, or a dashboard. With a row focused, . (or Shift+F10) opens it too.

  • Rename.
  • Pinned to sidebar and Start view on this device: a check mark shows which apply.
  • Move up and Move down: unavailable at the top or bottom of the list, with the reason shown.
  • Delete view… asks for confirmation first. Deleting a view never touches your tasks.

Build a dashboard#

A dashboard puts up to six saved views side by side, each showing its count and first ten tasks. It's handy for a morning review: "Due this week", "Deep work" and "Waiting on others" on one screen.

Open the views list (g v), choose + New dashboard, name it, then add saved views as panels from the dashboard's header. On a phone the panels stack. Move between panels with Tab, and through a panel's tasks with j / k.

Choose where the app opens#

Each device can open on a different view: your laptop on a "Work" view, your phone on Today. Pick it in Settings → Preferences → Start view, or from a saved view's menu with Start view on this device. If that view is deleted later, the device opens on the Inbox and tells you why.

Tips#

  • Subtasks show up on their own in Today and Upcoming, with their parent's name next to them, so you see exactly what's due.
  • Views that sort by date (Today, Upcoming, labels, filters) can't be reordered by hand. Projects and the Inbox can.
  • Filter queries has ten ready-made examples to copy.

pages.title: Search and commands
pages.summary: One box on Ctrl+K finds any task, project, label, view or setting, runs any command by name, and understands filter queries.
pages.html:
Search and commands

Press Ctrl+K (⌘+K on a Mac) anywhere in the app to find anything or do anything by name. It also works while you are typing in a field, except in a task's notes, where the same keys insert a link.

Open the box#

Use the shortcut, or the magnifying glass at the top of the screen. On a phone the box opens as a sheet from the bottom. Type, move with ↑ and ↓, and press Enter; Esc closes it and returns you where you were.

With nothing typed, the box lists what you can do right now (for the selected task, the project or view you are in) and what you picked most recently on this device.

What it finds#

  • Tasks, by title and by the text of their notes. Open tasks come first; completed ones are marked. Deleted tasks never show up. Picking a task opens its project with the task's panel open.
  • Projects (archived ones are marked), labels, saved views and dashboards, and the Settings sections you can see.

Matching ignores case and accents and finds words by their start or by letters in order: cafe finds Café, rp finds Renew passport. Exact matches come first, then word starts, then the rest; among equal matches, what you picked often on this device comes first. At most 50 results are listed; keep typing to narrow them down.

Filter queries inline#

If what you type is a filter query, such as @errand & p1, due <= friday or #Work & overdue, the box lists the matching tasks and offers Open in Filter view. Plain words are always a text search, so a half-typed query never shows an error.

Commands#

Every action has a name in the box: go to any view, calendar or Settings section; act on the selected task (complete, priority, labels, assign, estimate, deadline, defer, park, This Evening, schedule, skip an occurrence, move to the Trash); act on the project, saved view, label or section you are in (everything in their menus, such as Pin to sidebar or Archive); save the current filter as a view; create a task, project, label or dashboard; sync now; show the keyboard shortcuts; turn Vim keybindings on or off; search Help for what you typed. Each command shows its shortcut, so the box also teaches the keys.

Commands are listed only when they apply: with no task selected there are no task commands, and a viewer of a shared project doesn't see the ones that would change it.

Privacy#

The search runs on your device, over the data already stored there. Nothing you type is sent to the server, and nothing is indexed on it. This works offline and for end-to-end encrypted accounts too: your device holds the decrypted text and searches that.

pages.title: Sections and boards
pages.summary: Split a project into stages with sections, and switch it to a board to move cards between columns by drag or keyboard.

toc.text: Rename, reorder or delete a section
Get around the board with the keyboard

pages.html:
Sections and boards

Sections divide a project into parts, like "Planning", "In progress" and "Waiting", or "Kitchen", "Bathroom" and "Garden". The same project can be shown as a list with headings or as a board with one column per section.

Add a section#

Open a project and select + Add section at the bottom of the list. Type a name and press Enter. You can add the next one straight away.

Each heading shows how many open tasks it holds. Tasks without a section are listed first under No section.

Add tasks to a section#

Select the + on a section heading and type: the task goes straight into that section. You can also open any task and choose a Section in its panel.

Rename, reorder or delete a section#

Use the ⋯ menu on a section heading (or press . with the heading focused):

  • Rename (F2)
  • Move it up or down (left or right on the board). At the first or last place the option is unavailable and says why.
  • Delete section… asks first and says how many open tasks move to No section. The tasks aren't deleted.

Fold a section with the small arrow next to its name. Folding is remembered on that device only.

Switch to a board#

At the top of the project, choose Board (or press v). Each section becomes a column, with No section first. Press v again, or choose List, to switch back.

The choice is remembered for each project on each device. Your laptop can show "Q4 launch" as a board while your phone shows it as a list. On a narrow screen the board scrolls sideways.

Move cards between columns#

  • Drag a card to another column, or to a place within a column. On a touch screen, press and hold the card first.
  • Keyboard: select a card and press Shift+→ or Shift+←. The card stays selected, so you can keep moving it.
  • Panel: open the task and pick another Section.

Moving with the keyboard or the panel puts the card at the bottom of the new column.

Get around the board with the keyboard#

Key Does
h / l or ← / → Jump to the previous or next column
j / k Move up and down within a column
Shift+← / Shift+→ Move the selected card to the previous or next column
a Add a task to the selected card's column
Enter Open the card

Good to know#

  • Moving a task to another project removes it from its section, because sections belong to one project.
  • If someone deletes a section while you were moving a task into it on another device, the task ends up under No section. Nothing is lost.
  • Sections are part of the export and come back when you import it.

Ideas for sections#

  • A simple flow: To do, Doing, Done.
  • By place: Kitchen, Bathroom, Garden for a renovation.
  • By week: This week, Next week, Later for a launch plan.

pages.title: Attachments
pages.summary: Add files and links to tasks and comments, offline included; limits, who can see and remove them, encryption and where the files live.

toc.text: Add a file or a link

pages.html:
Attachments

A task, or a comment on it, can carry files and links: a receipt, a photo of a whiteboard, a PDF, the link to a design. Open a task and use Attachments below its subtasks, or the paperclip in the comment box.

Add a file or a link#

  • Pick, paste or drop. Choose Add file to pick files, paste an image or a file into the task panel, or drop files onto it.
  • Links. Choose Add link and paste an http or https address. A link is stored as a link: the server never downloads it.
  • Offline. Adding a file without a connection works: the attachment appears at once, marked "waiting to upload", and uploads after the next sync. Other devices show it as "uploading" until the file has arrived on the server.

Images show a thumbnail; other files show their name, type and size. Open shows the file in a new tab when the browser can display it safely (images, PDF, plain text, audio and video); everything else, and every file of an encrypted account, is downloaded instead. You can rename your own attachments and remove them; a removal can be undone from the notice that follows.

Who sees and changes them#

Attachments belong to their task: everyone who can see the task can see its attachments, viewers of a shared project included, and anyone who can comment can attach files. Only the person who added an attachment can rename it. The author, a project admin and the owner can remove it.

Limits#

The server owner sets a size limit per file (25 MB unless changed) and a total per account (1 GB unless changed) in Settings → Administration → Attachments, and can turn attachments off. Settings → Data shows how much of your total you use. Removing an attachment frees your total at once; the file itself stays on the server for the Trash retention period (30 days unless changed), so a removal can be undone from any device, and is then deleted for good. Purging a task from the Trash deletes its files immediately.

Encryption#

On an account with end-to-end encryption, the file name, its type, a link's address and the file's bytes are encrypted on your device before they leave it. The server stores and serves only the encrypted bytes and never holds a key. Turning encryption on or off re-uploads existing files in the new form as part of the switch.

Privacy and safety#

Files are only ever served to signed-in people who can see the task. A file is never shown as a web page: documents that could run code (HTML, SVG and the like) are always downloaded, and every file is served with headers that stop the browser from running anything in it.

For operators#

Files live under <data>/attachments/, one file per attachment, written once and never changed. Backups include them after the database, the ZIP export (GET /api/v1/export?format=zip) adds them to a user's export, and opentodo restore puts them back. The optional OPENTODO_ATTACHMENTS_MAX_FILE_MB and OPENTODO_ATTACHMENTS_QUOTA_MB preset the two limits on the first start; after that the owner's settings decide. The public demo has attachments turned off. The routes are described in the API reference.

pages.title: Labels and filters
pages.summary: Tag tasks across projects with labels, then find exactly what you need with the filter language and save it as a view.

toc.text: Add a label to a task
Save a filter as a view

pages.html:
Labels and filters

Projects say where a task belongs. Labels say what kind of task it is, across all projects: @call, @errand, @waiting, @deep-work. Filters then let you ask questions like "every call I need to make this week".

Add a label to a task#

Pick whichever is quickest:

  • Type it in quick add: Phone the bank @call.
  • Select a task and press L, start typing, and press Enter. The picker stays open so you can add more.
  • Open the task and use Labels in the panel.

If the label doesn't exist yet, typing its name and pressing Enter creates it. Labels show as small colored chips on the task. To remove one, open the task and select the × on the chip.

See everything with one label#

The Labels group in the sidebar lists your labels with the number of open tasks for each. Select one to see all its tasks, grouped by project.

All next to Labels (or g l) opens the labels page: every label with its colour, its number of open tasks, a drag handle and a ⋯ menu. The sidebar rows have the same menu.

Rename, recolour and reorder#

  • Rename: double-click a label, or focus it and press F2. A name another label already has is refused, and the old name stays.
  • Edit… in the menu opens a panel with the name, the colour swatches (arrow keys move between them), and buttons to move the label.
  • Reorder: drag a label by its handle (on a phone, press and hold the handle so scrolling the list still works), or focus it and press Alt+↑ / Alt+↓. Alt+Shift+↑ / ↓ moves it to the top or bottom. The new position is announced to screen readers.
  • . or Shift+F10 opens the menu of the focused label.

Merge and delete#

  • Merge into…: type to find the label to keep. A confirmation names both labels and how many tasks change. Tasks with the first label get the second one instead, and the first is deleted. Handy when you end up with both "Errand" and "errand".
  • Delete label…: the confirmation says how many tasks carry it. It's removed from them; the tasks stay.

If two of your devices created the same label while offline, both copies get a duplicate badge, and the labels page offers to merge them. Swap chooses which one is kept.

Every change is saved on this device first and syncs to your other devices, also when you make it offline.

Labels are personal. In a shared project, other members don't see the labels you add.

Find tasks with a filter#

Open Filter in the sidebar (or press g f) and type a query. Results appear as you type, grouped by project.

A query combines small pieces:

Piece Means Example
@name has this label @call
#name in this project #Work
##name in this project or its sub-projects ##Work
p1 … p4 priority p1
today, tomorrow, overdue, no date due then, or not at all overdue
due <= 7 days due within the next week due before friday
search: text words in the title or notes search: invoice
blocked, unblocked waiting for an open task, or not unblocked & today
completed include completed tasks #Home & completed

Join them with & (and), | (or) and ! (not), and use brackets to group:

(@call | @errand) & due <= 7 days

That reads: tasks labeled call or errand, due within the next seven days. A few more:

  • #Work & p1 & due <= tomorrow: the most important work for today and tomorrow.
  • overdue & no project: overdue tasks still sitting in the Inbox.
  • @waiting & !#Work: everything you're waiting on, outside work.

Names with spaces go in quotes: #"Client A". Upper and lower case don't matter. If you mistype, a message under the box says where, and the previous results stay visible.

Press Enter to jump from the box to the first result, and Esc to go back. ↑ and ↓ in the box bring back your recent queries.

The full language, with ten worked examples, is in Filter queries.

Save a filter as a view#

When a query is useful, keep it: press s in the results, give it a name, and it appears under Views in the sidebar with a live count. Saved views sync to your other devices. See Views for grouping, sorting and dashboards.

Tips#

  • Labels for context work well: @call, @computer, @errand, @home. Then a view like @errand & due <= 2 days is your shopping list.
  • A @waiting label plus a pinned "Waiting on others" view makes follow-ups hard to forget.
  • Filters run on your device. They're instant, and they work offline.

pages.title: Recurring tasks and reminders
pages.summary: Make a task repeat every week, month or weekday, skip an occurrence, and get reminded at the right moment.

toc.text: Complete, skip or split off one occurrence

pages.html:
Recurring tasks and reminders

Some tasks come back: pay the rent, water the plants, the weekly one-to-one. Make them repeat once and OpenTodo moves them forward each time you complete them. Add a reminder and you'll get a nudge when it matters.

Make a task repeat#

Open the task and type a rule into Repeat, such as every week. A list of suggestions appears as you type. Under the field you'll see the next three dates, so you can check the rule does what you meant.

Set a rule in the task panel under Repeat, or type it straight into quick add: Water plants every Monday creates the task with the rule and its first date. See Repeat and remind for the phrases in each language.

Repeating tasks show a ↻ symbol on the row. To stop repeating, select the × next to the rule.

Rules you can write#

Rule Repeats
every day, every 3 days daily, or every few days
every weekday Monday to Friday
every week, every 2 weeks weekly or fortnightly
every monday, every mon, wed, fri on those weekdays
every month, every 15th monthly, on the same day or a fixed day
every last day, every last friday at the end of the month
every 2nd tuesday the second Tuesday of each month
every year once a year on the same date

Two extras work with any of these:

  • After completion: every 2 weeks after completion counts from the day you actually finish, not from the due date. Good for things like "change the water filter".
  • An end: add until 2026-12-31 or for 10 times to stop the series.

Rules are stored in English, whichever language you typed them in. Every detail is in the recurring task rules reference.

Complete, skip or split off one occurrence#

When you complete a repeating task, that occurrence is recorded in Completed, and the task moves to its next date. If it was overdue, it jumps to the next date from today, so missed occurrences don't pile up.

The buttons under the rule handle the exceptions:

  • Skip (Shift+S) moves to the next date without recording a completion. Use it when this week's run is cancelled.
  • This occurrence only (Shift+O) splits the current occurrence off as a normal task you can change freely, while the series moves on. Use it when this week's meeting is on Thursday instead.

Changing the title, notes, project, priority, labels or time of a repeating task changes the whole series.

Add a reminder#

Open a task and select + Add reminder under Reminders. Choose one of:

  • At due time, 10 minutes before, 30 minutes before, 1 hour before or 1 day before,
  • Custom offset…, for any number of minutes, hours or days before or after,
  • once the task has a deadline: On the deadline, 1 day before the deadline or Custom before the deadline…. These count from 09:00 on the deadline day and follow the deadline, not the due date,
  • At a specific date and time…, for a fixed moment that doesn't depend on the due date. Its date and time fields work like the ones under Due: type the date and time in your format or pick them from the calendar and the list of times (see Dates and times).

Reminders are listed with their day, date and time in your format, for example Tue 3 Nov, 09:00. A task can have several reminders. Reminders relative to the due time move with it: change the due date and they follow, and on a repeating task they carry over to the next occurrence. If the task has a date but no time, "before" and "after" count from 09:00 that day.

When a reminder goes off#

While OpenTodo is open, a reminder pops up in the corner of the screen with Snooze 10 min, 1 hour, Tomorrow 09:00 and Dismiss. This works without a connection and without any permission.

To get reminders when the app is closed, turn on notifications for each device in Settings → Notifications. On an iPhone this needs the installed app. See Notifications.

Snoozing or dismissing on one device applies to all of them.

Shared projects#

Reminders are personal. On a task in a shared project, your reminders are yours alone: other members don't see them and don't get them. You can add reminders even if you can only view the project.

Tips#

  • For bills, use a day-of-month rule (every 1st) plus a 1 day before reminder.
  • A reminder on a task without a time fires at 09:00 for "at due time". Give the task a time if you need it earlier.
  • Deleted tasks don't remind you. If you restore one, its reminders come back.

pages.title: Time blocking
pages.summary: Estimate how long tasks take, then place them on the Day or Week calendar to see whether your plan fits the day.

toc.text: Estimate how long a task takes
Place a task on the calendar

pages.html:
Time blocking

A to-do list tells you what to do. A calendar tells you when. Time blocking puts the two together: give tasks an estimate, drop them on the Day or Week calendar, and you can see at a glance whether your day is realistic.

Estimate how long a task takes#

Select a task and press e, then type 20, 45m, 1h or 1h30 and press Enter. In the task panel, Estimate also has buttons for 15 minutes up to 2 hours. In quick add, write +30m or +1h30.

The estimate shows on the task row, like 45m or 1h 30m.

Open the calendar#

Choose Day or Week in the sidebar, or press g d or g w.

  • Tasks with a date and a time appear as blocks at that time. The block is as tall as the estimate.
  • A timed task without an estimate gets a 30-minute block with a dashed outline.
  • Tasks with a date but no time wait in the Unscheduled lane at the top of their day.
  • A red line marks the current time.

Use ‹ and › (or [ and ]) to go back and forward, and Today (or t) to come back.

The Week view starts on your first day of the week, and the hours and block times follow your time format (9 AM or 09:00). Both are set in Settings → Preferences → Date and time and follow you to all your devices. Moving a block still sets the same time; only how it is shown changes.

Place a task on the calendar#

Drag a task from the Unscheduled lane onto a time slot. Its due date and time become that slot. The grid works in 15-minute steps.

To plan from your lists, open the side list with Plan from a list and drag tasks from there onto the calendar.

To change how long something takes, drag the bottom edge of its block. Dropping a block back on the Unscheduled lane keeps the date and removes the time.

With the keyboard#

Every move works without a mouse.

  1. In Today, a project or any list, select a task and press s. The Day view opens with the task ready to place.
  2. Move it with the arrow keys: ↑ / ↓ by 15 minutes, ← / → by a day.
  3. Press Enter to place it, or Esc to cancel.

On the calendar itself, j / k select tasks, the arrows move the selected one, Shift+↑ / Shift+↓ shorten or lengthen it, and u takes it off the grid while keeping its date.

See whether the day fits#

Each day's header adds up the estimates of its open tasks and compares them with your day length, for example 4h 15m / 8h. When you've planned more than the day holds, the header is marked as over capacity. That's your cue to move something.

Tasks that overlap in time are shown side by side, with a marker, so nothing hides behind something else.

Completing a task removes its block and lowers the day's total.

Adjust the grid#

In Settings → Preferences → Calendar you can set when the grid starts and ends (6:00 to 22:00 by default; you can still scroll beyond) and how long your working day is (8 hours by default). These settings belong to each device, so your phone and laptop can differ.

Tips#

  • Estimate generously at first. After a week you'll know how long "quick" things really take.
  • Leave gaps. A day planned to the minute falls apart at the first phone call.
  • The Quick wins button above your lists shows tasks of 15 minutes or less, good for filling a short gap.
  • Dates and times you set on the calendar are ordinary due dates, so they show up in Today and Upcoming as well, and in calendar apps connected over CalDAV.

pages.title: Sharing and comments
pages.summary: Share a project with people on your server, choose what they can do, assign tasks, and talk it through in comments with @mentions.

toc.text: Leave or hand over a project

pages.html:
Sharing and comments

Projects can be shared with other people who have an account on the same OpenTodo server: your partner for the house move, your team for a launch. Everyone sees the same tasks, edits sync to everyone within seconds, and each task has a comment thread.

Share a project#

  1. Open the project and select Share at the top (or press Shift+S).
  2. Type the person's email address.
  3. Pick a role and select Share.

The project appears on their devices the next time they sync, with all its tasks. Shared projects have a small people icon in the sidebar.

Adding by email works only for people who already have an account on your server. For anyone else, send an invite link (next section).

Invite with a link#

An invite link adds one person to the project, whether or not they have an account yet.

  1. Open Share and select Create a link… under Invite with a link.
  2. Pick the role they get. Owners can also invite admins; admins can invite viewers and editors.
  3. Optionally enter their email: then only an account with that address can use the link.
  4. Choose how long it stays valid (1 hour to 30 days, 7 days by default) and select Create link.
  5. Select Copy link and send it however you like. OpenTodo never sends it for you.

The link is shown only once and works once. The dialog lists the links that are still waiting, with their role, email, expiry and who created them; Revoke stops one from working. Creating and revoking links need a connection.

When the person opens the link they see who invited them, the project and the role:

  • Already have an account? They select Sign in to join, sign in (with single sign-on too), and select Join project. Someone who is signed in already just selects Join project.
  • New to the server? They select Create an account, choose a name and password, and land in the project. This option appears only when the link is allowed to create accounts (see below). Otherwise the page tells them to get an account on the server first, then come back and sign in.

A link stops working when it expires, is revoked or has been used, when the project is deleted, or when the person who created it is no longer the project's owner or an admin. Someone who is already a member is told so, and the link stays unused for whoever it was meant for.

Who can bring new people#

New accounts are created through a project link only when one of these is true:

  • the link was created by the owner or an admin of the server;
  • open sign-up is on for the server;
  • the server owner switched on Members can invite new people with project links in Settings → Access policies → Project invite links. It is off by default.

When none applies, the Share dialog says so under the new link: it then works only for people who already have an account. The switch is checked when a link is used, so turning it on or off also affects links that were already sent.

Choose a role#

Role Can
viewer see the project and its tasks, and comment
editor also add, edit, complete and delete tasks, and assign them
admin also rename, recolor and archive the project, and manage members
owner everything, including deleting the project and handing it over

Every project has exactly one owner. To change someone's role, open Share and pick a new one next to their name. Remove takes them out of the project.

For viewers, the project is read-only: the add box and edit controls are switched off, with a note saying so.

Invite someone new#

Sign-up on an OpenTodo server is closed by default. The quickest way to bring someone into one project is an invite link. To invite someone to the server without a project, if you're the owner or an admin of the server, go to Settings → Administration → Members, optionally enter their email, choose how long the link stays valid, and select Create invitation. Copy the link and send it to them however you like; OpenTodo doesn't send emails. The link works once.

If you're not an admin of the server and your invite link can't create accounts, ask whoever runs it to invite the person, or to switch on Members can invite new people with project links. Once they've joined, you can share projects with them yourself.

Leave or hand over a project#

  • Leave: in the Share dialog, select Leave next to your own name. The project disappears from your devices; everyone else keeps it.
  • Make owner: the owner can hand the project to another member. The previous owner becomes an admin. Owners can't leave until they've done this.

When someone leaves or is removed, tasks assigned to them become unassigned.

Assign tasks#

In a shared project, each task can be assigned to one member. Open the task and choose someone under Assignee, or select the task and press Shift+A, type a name and press Enter. The assignee's avatar shows on the row, and they get a notification.

Assigned to me in the sidebar (g a) lists every open task assigned to you, across projects.

In your Inbox, in a project you haven't shared, or in a shared project where you are the only member, nobody else can be assigned, so the Assignee row reads You. That is only how the panel shows it: such a task is not in Assigned to me unless you turn on Show in Assigned to me in the same row, which assigns it to you. Turning it off unassigns it again. When you share the project with someone, its unassigned tasks read Unassigned from then on, and the tasks you assigned to yourself stay yours.

Comment on a task#

Open a task: Comments is the first tab below its details, next to Activity and History, and the panel remembers the tab you used last on this device. Press Shift+C with the task open to jump to the comment box from any tab. Comments read like a chat, oldest first, with the box at the end. Write your comment and post it with Comment or Ctrl+Enter (⌘+Enter on a Mac). If you close the task before sending, your draft is still there when you open it again on this device.

  • Mention someone by typing @ and picking their name. They get a notification.
  • Reply to a comment to keep a conversation together. The comment box shows who you're replying to, with a button to cancel and post a new comment instead. Replies are nested under the comment.
  • Edit or Delete your own comments; deleting asks you to confirm. Edited comments are marked as edited. Project admins and the owner can delete any comment. On a computer these actions appear when you point at a comment or move to it with the keyboard; on a phone they're always shown.
  • Hover over or focus a comment's time ("2 h ago") to see the full date and time in your format.
  • Comments support simple formatting: **bold**, *italic*, `code`, lists, quotes and links.

Everyone who can see a task can comment on it, viewers included. Rows with comments show a speech bubble and a count. Comments work offline too and are sent when you're back online.

The Activity tab shows the task's changes: who created it, completed it or changed its date. See Activity on a task.

See what others changed#

Activity in the sidebar (g h) lists the latest changes in all your shared projects, newest first and grouped by day. Each shared project shows a count of unread changes next to its name, and opening the feed marks them as seen. Filter by project, person or kind of change (completed, created, commented, assigned, rescheduled).

Inside a project, Activity at the top (Shift+H) shows the changes for that project only.

Things to know#

  • Labels and reminders stay personal. Labels you add to a shared task are only visible to you, and so are your reminders.
  • Moving a task out of a shared project to your own project or Inbox makes a copy there and removes the original from the shared project for everyone.
  • Deleting a shared project is something only the owner can do. It disappears for every member, and its open tasks are copied into the owner's Inbox.
  • End-to-end encryption and sharing don't mix. Shared projects are never encrypted, and an account with encryption turned on can't share new projects.

pages.title: Use AI with OpenTodo
pages.summary: Three ways to bring an AI assistant to your tasks: the assistant in the app, an assistant you already use over MCP, or a coding agent with the ot command. Which to pick and what each can touch.

toc.text: What every option has in common

pages.html:
Use AI with OpenTodo

OpenTodo doesn't come with an AI of its own and never sends your tasks anywhere by itself. You bring the model, and you decide what it can see and change. There are three ways to do it, and you can use any mix of them.

In the app Your assistant (MCP) A coding agent (ot)
Where you talk to it A chat panel in OpenTodo (Shift+I) Claude Desktop, an IDE or any MCP client A terminal agent or an automation script
Which model Anthropic, OpenAI, Gemini or a model on your own network, chosen by the server owner Whatever your assistant uses Whatever your agent uses
Who pays The key the owner (or you, if allowed) enters in Settings Your assistant's own plan Your agent's own plan
Changes Proposed, you review and apply them, one step undoes them Off by default; with an agent token, applied directly and undoable from history Same as MCP, plus --dry-run to preview
Set up by The server owner turns it on once You create a token and add one entry to your assistant's config You create a token and run ot auth set-token
Guide AI assistant AI assistants (MCP) Using ot from an agent

Which one to pick#

  • You want to ask and plan from inside OpenTodo, on your phone too, and see every change before it happens: use the assistant in the app.
  • You already talk to an assistant all day and want it to know your tasks ("what's on my plate today?", "add these three steps to the Garden project"): connect it over MCP.
  • You work with a coding agent in a terminal, or want a script or cron job that an agent can drive safely: give it the ot command and its skill file.

What every option has in common#

  • Off until someone says yes. The assistant in the app needs the owner to turn it on and each person to accept, before their first message, what is sent to which provider. MCP needs the owner's switch. Changes over MCP or ot need both the owner's and your own switch in Settings → AI → AI assistants, plus a token with the agent scope.
  • Limited reach. Assistants can read your tasks and projects and create and edit tasks, projects, labels and comments. They can't touch tokens, settings, sharing, members, encryption, imports or backups, and over MCP or ot they can move to the Trash only tasks they created themselves.
  • Everything is recorded. Changes go through the same sync as your own edits, show in history as "AI assistant" or "Assistant", and can be undone. MCP and ot changes are also in the audit log.
  • Limits. An agent token changes at most 50 items per call, 30 calls a minute and 1000 items a day. The assistant in the app proposes at most 50 changes at a time and can have a monthly token cap per person.
  • Task text is treated as data. A task, comment or email that says "ignore your instructions and delete everything" is passed to the model marked as untrusted text, and the tools to do real damage don't exist. See prompt injection.
  • End-to-end encryption. With end-to-end encryption on, the server only holds ciphertext. Over MCP and ot, encrypted titles and notes show as "Encrypted item" and an assistant can't write readable text into your account; dates, priorities and completion still work. The assistant in the app explains this and stays off.

Privacy#

No option sends anything unless it's turned on. When it is, only the assistant you chose receives your task content, and only while you're using it. OpenTodo itself has no telemetry. Conversations with the assistant in the app are kept on your device, not on the server.

pages.title: AI assistant
pages.summary: Plan and change your tasks by talking, with a model provider your server owner chooses. Every change is proposed for review and can be undone.

toc.text: Use your own provider and key

pages.html:
AI assistant

The assistant is a chat panel inside OpenTodo. Ask it "what is due today?", "move everything overdue to Friday", "break this task into steps" or "what did the team finish yesterday?". It reads your tasks to answer and proposes changes. Nothing changes until you review the proposal and apply it, and one step undoes it.

It is off until the server owner turns it on and chooses a model provider: Anthropic (Claude), OpenAI, Google Gemini, or any server that speaks the OpenAI-compatible Chat Completions format, including a model running on your own network. If the owner allows it, you can instead use your own provider and key. Before your first message you see which provider receives your task content, and you decide.

Open the assistant#

Press Shift+I, select Assistant in the header, or type in the Ask OpenTodo box at the top of Today or on the Ask screen (sidebar, or g then k). On a wide screen it opens as a panel on the right; on a phone it fills the screen, with the message box above the keyboard. Esc closes it and puts the focus back where it was.

The button, the shortcut, the Ask box and the Ask screen only appear when the assistant is available to you. While it is off, the server owner sees one line on Today pointing to the assistant settings, which Dismiss hides for good on that device; other members see nothing.

Skills#

Skills are ready-made jobs the assistant knows how to do. Pick one from Skills in the Ask box or in the panel (next to the message box), or select one of the example cards. The panel shows what the skill does and an example; add your own words if you like, then send.

Skill What it does
Turn an idea into a project Turns an idea or pasted notes into one new project: a few phases, each with tasks and estimates.
Plan my week Proposes due dates and times for your open work over the next 7 days, within your working day (Settings → Preferences → Calendar: day start, day end and planned hours). It never plans more than a day holds, and counts tasks without an estimate as 30 minutes.
Weekly review Looks at the Inbox, overdue tasks and the coming week, and proposes what to reschedule, move or complete, with a short summary. It never proposes trashing your tasks.
Triage my inbox Proposes a project, and a priority, labels and a date where the task gives a reason, for each Inbox task.
Break this down Turns the selected task into subtasks with estimates. Also in a task's ⋯ menu.

A skill can only use the tools it needs (Break this down cannot move or complete anything), and what it proposes is reviewed, applied and undone exactly like any other answer.

Paste notes#

Paste meeting notes, an email or a list into the Ask box or the message box and it is kept apart as pasted text: the assistant uses it as material, never as instructions. If the text contains instructions ("ignore your rules…"), the assistant ignores them and says so. Pasted text counts toward the 256 KB limit of one message.

Before your first message#

The panel first shows what will be sent and to whom:

  • the provider and model the owner chose, or the provider you chose with your own key,
  • what may be sent: task titles and descriptions; project, section and label names; due dates, priorities and completion; comments; the names, types and links of attachments (never the files); names of members of shared projects; your display name, today's date and your time zone; and the messages you type.

In a shared project that includes text other members wrote. Select Accept and continue to start. Nothing is sent to any provider before you accept. If the provider changes later (the owner switches, you choose your own, or the owner stops allowing members' own keys), the assistant asks you again. You can withdraw consent in Settings → AI → Assistant.

Use your own provider and key#

When the server owner turns on Let members bring their own key, Settings → AI → Assistant shows Which assistant you use:

  • The server's assistant: the provider and model the owner set up. This is the default.
  • My own provider and key: choose Anthropic (Claude), OpenAI or Google Gemini, a model, and paste an API key from your own account, then select Save my provider. For Anthropic you pick one of the offered models; for OpenAI and Gemini you type the model id (up to 100 characters: letters, digits, ., _, : and -, for example gpt-4.1-mini or gemini-2.5-flash). Test connection sends one tiny request with the provider, model and key on screen to check them, before or after you save (up to 5 tests in 10 minutes). Testing never saves anything.

Your questions then go from this server to the provider you chose, with your key, so that provider's terms for your account apply. The assistant asks you to accept the disclosure for that provider before your next message. Your key is stored on the server, never shown again, never sent to your browser and never in backups or exports. Going back to The server's assistant deletes the key you stored for your provider.

A compatible endpoint (a model server address) is never offered here: only the server owner decides which other machines the server connects to.

If the owner later stops allowing members' own keys, your choice is kept but not used: the server's assistant answers (after you accept its disclosure) until the owner allows it again. Forget my provider and key deletes both.

If you saved a key in an earlier version of OpenTodo, it still works with the server's assistant; Remove my key deletes it.

Ask and review#

Type a question and press Enter (Shift+Enter adds a line). The answer appears as it is written; lines such as "Looking at Today…" show what the assistant is reading. Screen readers hear the answer a sentence at a time.

When you ask for changes, the answer ends with Proposed changes: one line per task or project, each change in words ("Due Sun 11 Oct → Fri 16 Oct", "Completed", "New task in Garden: Buy seeds").

  • Every item is checked. Uncheck what you do not want.
  • Apply (or Enter inside the list) applies the checked items. The summary says how many were applied ("4 of 5 changes applied").
  • Discard (or Esc inside the list) drops the proposal. Nothing changes.
  • Items in a shared project are marked, because other people see the change.
  • An item that changed on another device after it was proposed is unchecked and marked changed since proposed. Applying the rest leaves the newer value alone.
  • An item that no longer exists on this device is left out with a note.

One proposal holds at most 50 changes. For bigger requests the assistant proposes the first 50 and offers to continue after you have reviewed them.

Applied changes are ordinary edits made on this device: they show at once, work offline, sync to your other devices, appear in the task's history as Assistant, and trigger reminders, webhooks and notifications like any edit.

Undo#

After applying, Undo appears in the panel and in a short notice at the bottom of the screen. It puts back every value the proposal changed and moves tasks it created to the Trash, in one step, also offline. If you edited one of those fields again in the meantime, your edit stays and the undo names that task. The last 20 applied proposals on a device can be undone.

Apply small changes without review#

The switch Settings → AI → Assistant → Apply small changes without review (this device) is off by default. When it is on, a proposal that touches at most 3 existing tasks and only changes completion, due dates, priority or labels is applied at once, with an Undo notice. Anything else, including every new task, every move to another project or section, every deletion and every text edit, is always shown for review.

Conversations stay on this device#

Conversations are stored only in this browser: never synced, never sent to other people, not in exports or backups. The panel keeps the last 50 conversations for up to 30 days. History lists them (also offline), New starts another, and Clear conversations deletes them (also Settings → AI → Assistant → Clear conversations on this device, which asks you to confirm). Signing out deletes them too. The server keeps nothing of a conversation after it has answered.

Offline you can read earlier conversations and apply or undo a proposal that already arrived; asking needs a connection.

Costs and limits#

Each answer shows how many tokens it used and how much of your monthly allowance that is ("1,240 tokens · this month 18% of your limit"); Settings → AI → Assistant shows the month so far. The owner sets the allowance (500,000 tokens per person per month by default). When you reach it, the assistant says when it resets (the first day of the next month, UTC). One answer at a time per person.

Answers on your own key are paid by you, so they do not count toward the allowance and are never stopped by it ("1,240 tokens · your key"); Settings shows them separately. The owner can choose to count them as well.

Safety#

  • You confirm every change. The assistant cannot change anything by itself: the server never applies its proposals; your device does, after you review them (or, for the small changes above, when you turned that on).
