pages.html:
Recurring task rules

A task can repeat. The rule is a short English phrase stored in the task's recurrence field, for example every weekday or every 3 days after completion. The same grammar is implemented by the server (internal/recurrence) and the web app (web/src/lib/recurrence.ts), and both are tested against one shared file of test vectors (web/src/lib/recurrence.vectors.json), so every device and the REST API compute the same dates. Every example on this page is one of those vectors.

Grammar#

every <pattern> [after completion] [until YYYY-MM-DD | for N times]

Rules are case-insensitive and extra whitespace is ignored. A rule is at most 200 characters. What gets stored is the canonical form: lowercase, single spaces, weekday names spelled out, ordinals with the correct suffix. Every 2nd Tuesday is stored as every 2nd tuesday.

Pattern Examples Meaning
day, N days every day, every 3 days Daily, or every N days (1–999).
week, N weeks every week, every 2 weeks Every 7 × N days.
weekday every weekday Monday to Friday.
month, N months every month, every 6 months Same day of month; a day the month does not have becomes its last day.
year, N years every year, every 2 years Same date; 29 February becomes 28 February in common years.
weekday names every monday, every mon, wed, fri, every tuesday and thursday Any set of weekdays, full names or three-letter abbreviations, separated by commas or "and".
day of month every 1st, every 15th, every 31st That day of each month; in shorter months the last day.
last day every last day The last day of each month.
last weekday every last weekday The last Monday–Friday of each month.
ordinal weekday every 2nd tuesday, every first monday, every last friday 1st/first to 4th/fourth or last of that weekday in each month.

every 2nd is the 2nd day of each month; every 2nd tuesday is the second Tuesday.

Completion-relative rules#

Add after completion to a day, week, month or year interval to count from the day the task is actually completed instead of from its due date: every 3 days after completion, every week after completion. Calendar patterns (weekdays, days of month, ordinals) cannot be completion-relative.

End conditions#

  • until YYYY-MM-DD: no occurrence after that date, e.g. every day until 2026-12-31.
  • for N times: the series has N occurrences in total, e.g. every weekday for 10 times. Skipped occurrences do not count.

Only one end condition per rule.

How the next occurrence is computed#

All dates are floating calendar dates (YYYY-MM-DD), like due itself; the computation never converts through a time zone, so daylight saving changes have no effect. The due time, if any, is kept.

A deadline on the series moves by the same number of days as the due date: every monday due 12 October with the deadline 14 October is next due 19 October with the deadline 21 October, also when an overdue series catches up. Skipping and "this occurrence only" move it the same way. The completed occurrence and a detached copy keep the deadline they had. A start date moves the same way, so a task deferred until two days before it is due is deferred again before the next occurrence. This Evening stays on the series. Parking a repeating task in Someday clears its due date and so ends the repetition.

  • Calendar rules: the next occurrence is the first matching date strictly after the current due date. If that date is already in the past (the task was overdue), it is instead the first matching date after today: overdue tasks catch up rather than piling up, and no missed occurrences are generated. Interval rules keep their rhythm while catching up (every 3 days due on the 1st, completed on the 10th, moves to the 13th).
  • Completion-relative rules: the next occurrence is counted from the local date of completion. every 3 days after completion due Monday and completed on Wednesday is next due Saturday; completed on the Sunday before, it is next due Wednesday.
  • Month ends: every month due 31 January moves to 28 (or 29) February. The rule has no memory of the original day, so the following month is the 28th too; use every 31st or every last day to stay at the end of the month.
  • A rule set on a task without a due date gives it one: the first matching date from today on.

Completing, skipping and editing#

  • Complete: a completed copy of the current occurrence (the occurrence record) goes to Completed, and the task moves to its next occurrence. When the end condition is reached the task completes like any other task.
  • Skip (Shift+S, or Skip in the detail panel): moves the task to the next occurrence without recording a completion. Completion-relative rules skip as if completed today. Skipping the last occurrence is not possible; complete or delete it.
  • This occurrence only (Shift+O, or the button in the detail panel): makes a standalone copy of the current occurrence, without a rule, and moves the series to its next occurrence. Edit or move the copy freely.
  • Every other edit (title, notes, project, priority, labels, due time, rule) applies to the series, because the series is the task.
  • Reopen an occurrence record and it becomes a standalone open task; the series is not moved back. Reopening a series that ended keeps its rule, so its next completion continues the schedule.

Sync and convergence#

The rule is stored in task.recurrence and occurrence records point back with task.series_id (see sync.md). An occurrence record's id is derived from the series id and the occurrence date (SHA-256, formatted as a UUID), and the next due date is a pure function of the rule and dates every device shares. Two devices that complete the same occurrence offline therefore write the same record and the same next due date, and end with one Completed entry once they sync. A for N times count is the number of occurrence records, so it converges without a counter.

The REST API behaves the same: PATCH /api/v1/tasks/{id} with a non-null completed_at on a recurring task records the occurrence and moves the task (see api.md).

Clients older than this feature keep working: they store the new fields without showing them and complete a recurring task as a plain completion, which is recovered by reopening it on an updated device.

pages.title: Reminders reference
pages.summary: How relative, deadline and absolute reminders fire, web push and its privacy, snooze, shared projects and the Trash.
pages.html:
Reminders reference

A task can carry any number of reminders (OpenSpec change reminders). Open a task, then use the Reminders section of the detail panel.

You can also type reminders in quick add: Dentist tomorrow at 15:00 remind me 30 min before (see Repeat and remind).

  • Relative reminders fire a number of minutes before or after the task's due time ("30 minutes before"). A task with a date but no time counts as due at 09:00. A task whose time is fixed to a time zone fires relative to that exact instant, wherever your devices are. When the due date or time changes, on any device or through the API, the reminder moves with it; recurring tasks carry their relative reminders to the next occurrence. Without a due date a relative reminder is kept but does not fire.
  • Deadline reminders fire a number of minutes before or after 09:00 on the task's deadline ("1 day before the deadline"), in your device's time zone. They follow the deadline when it changes, on any device or through the API, and never move with the due date. Without a deadline the reminder is kept but does not fire. A device on an older version leaves them untouched.
  • Absolute reminders fire at a moment you pick and never move with the due date. They work on undated tasks and are shown in each device's local time.

Shared projects#

Reminders are personal. On a task in a shared project your reminders are yours alone: other members never see or receive them, and you can add them with any role, viewer included. When someone else moves the task, your relative reminders follow as soon as one of your devices syncs.

Delivery#

In the app. While the app is open, a reminder whose time has come appears as a notification in the corner with Snooze 10 min, 1 hour, Tomorrow 09:00 and Dismiss (focus moves to it; Esc dismisses). This needs no network and no permission, and is skipped for completed or deleted tasks. When the tab is in the background and the browser allows notifications, a system notification is shown instead.

Web push. In Settings → Notifications each device can enable push so reminders arrive while the app is closed. Enabling asks for the browser permission and registers the device with the server; disabling or signing out removes it. The server checks for due reminders every 30 seconds and sends each one once per firing time to every enabled device of the reminder's owner (reminders are personal), then records the delivery on the reminder (an op by device server) so all devices know it fired. System notifications offer Snooze 10 min and Dismiss; these work offline and are uploaded on the next sync. If the app is focused when a push arrives, the reminder is shown in the app only.

Privacy. A push payload carries only the reminder id, the task id and the firing time, encrypted end to end (RFC 8291) so the push service cannot read it. The device shows the title from its own copy of the task. Enable Include task titles if a device should be able to show the title before it has synced the task; the description is never sent.

Trash#

A reminder does not fire, in the app or by push, while its task is deleted or while the task's project, or any project above it, is in the Trash. It is not marked as delivered either, so restoring the task or the project brings it back: a reminder whose time is still ahead fires on time, and one whose time passed while it was in the Trash is delivered once, late, on the next check (the same rule as for reminders that fell due while the server was down). Dismiss or snooze it if you no longer need it. Purging the task from the Trash removes its reminders.

Snooze and dismiss#

Snoozing sets a new firing time (in 10 minutes, in an hour, or tomorrow at 09:00) and the reminder fires again, also by push. Dismissing silences the current firing. Both are ordinary synced edits: when one device dismisses and another later snoozes the same reminder, the later edit wins on every device.

End-to-end encryption#

For an account with end-to-end encryption the server never puts a title in a push, even for devices that opted in to titles: it cannot read it, and ciphertext would be useless. The notification uses the content-free text; in-app reminder toasts still show the decrypted title from the device.

For operators#

Nothing to configure. The VAPID key pair is generated on first use at <data>/push_vapid.pem and travels with backup archives. OPENTODO_PUSH=off turns push off entirely (routes answer 404, no outbound requests); in-app reminders keep working. Push requires the app to be served over https (OPENTODO_BASE_URL), as browsers only allow push subscriptions on secure origins. See self-hosting and API.

pages.title: Capturing pages
pages.summary: Save pages, selected text, files and screenshots from other apps: the share sheet, the bookmarklet and the browser extension.
pages.html:
Capturing pages

Many tasks start as "deal with this page later". OpenTodo can receive a page from three places, and all of them open the same capture screen at /share on your own server:

From How Works offline
Phone or desktop share sheet Install the app, then choose OpenTodo in the share menu Yes, once the app has been opened online
Any desktop browser The bookmarklet from Settings → Capture The popup opens from the app's offline cache once the app has been loaded in that browser
Chromium and Firefox The browser extension in extension/ Same as the bookmarklet

The capture screen proposes:

  • Title: the page title, or the link's host name when there is no title. The title field is a regular quick-add line, so typing tomorrow #work p1 into it sets the date, project and priority.
  • Description: the selected or shared text, followed by the link.
  • Project: the Inbox by default; pick any project.
  • Files: anything shared along with the page (photos, PDFs, documents) or a screenshot from the extension, each with its name, type and size and a thumbnail for images. Remove any you don't want; they're saved as attachments of the new task. A share that carries only a file proposes the file's name as the title.

Press Enter to save or Esc to cancel. Nothing is saved until you confirm. Saving creates an ordinary task on the device first and syncs it like any other quick-add task, so it works with no network and reaches your other devices when the network returns.

When the capture screen was opened as a popup (bookmarklet, extension) or in a window opened just for the share, it closes itself after Save or Esc. Otherwise it takes you to the Inbox or to the project you picked.

Share sheet (installed app)#

The web app manifest declares a Web Share Target (POST /share with title, text, url and files), so the app is offered for links, text, images and documents. The browser adds OpenTodo to the share menu once the app is installed:

Platform Install Share
Android, Chrome / Edge / Samsung Internet Menu → Install app (or Add to Home screen) Share from any app → OpenTodo
Windows, ChromeOS, Chrome / Edge Install icon in the address bar Share from apps that use the system share dialog
macOS, Chrome / Edge Install icon in the address bar Support for receiving shares varies by version; use the bookmarklet or extension
iOS and iPadOS, any browser Share → Add to Home Screen Safari does not support share targets for web apps; use the bookmarklet in Safari instead
Firefox (all platforms) Firefox does not install web apps as share targets Use the extension or bookmarklet

Some apps put the link inside the shared text instead of the link field. The capture screen then takes the last http(s) link from the text and moves it to the end of the description.

After an update that adds or changes the share target, the browser may need the app to be opened once (or reinstalled) before the share menu entry appears. If a share reaches the server before the app has been opened since the update, the title, text and link still arrive, and the capture screen says the files did not: open the app once and share again.

Shared files never leave the device before you save. The app's service worker receives the share on the device, also offline, and keeps the files in a separate local store (opentodo-share) only until the capture screen is saved or cancelled. Anything left there is removed after ten minutes and at sign-out. Saving creates the task and its attachments in one step, on the device first; the files upload with the next sync.

Bookmarklet#

Settings → Capture shows an Add to OpenTodo button generated for your server's address. Drag it to the bookmarks bar (or use Copy bookmarklet and paste the code as the address of a new bookmark). Clicking it on any page opens a small popup with the capture screen, prefilled with the page's address, title and the text you selected.

The bookmarklet contains no password or token. It only opens your server's /share page in a popup, where your normal sign-in applies. Its source, with your server's address in place of https://todo.example.com:

javascript:(function () {
  var e = encodeURIComponent
  var s = String(window.getSelection ? getSelection() : '').slice(0, 16384)
  var u = "https://todo.example.com/share" + '?url=' + e(location.href) + '&title=' + e(document.title) + (s ? '&text=' + e(s) : '')
  if (!window.open(u, 'opentodo-capture', 'popup,width=480,height=640'))
    alert('Allow pop-ups for this site to capture it to OpenTodo.')
})()

If nothing happens, the browser blocked the popup: allow pop-ups for the site you are on. Some sites block bookmarklets with their own security policy; the extension works there.

Browser extension#

extension/ holds a small Manifest V3 extension for Chromium-based browsers (Chrome, Edge, Brave, Vivaldi) and Firefox 121 or later. It adds:

  • a toolbar button Add to OpenTodo,
  • a context-menu entry Add to OpenTodo on pages and selections,
  • a keyboard shortcut, Alt+Shift+O by default (change it at chrome://extensions/shortcuts or in Firefox's Manage Extension Shortcuts).

Each opens your server's capture screen in a popup window with the current tab's address, title and selection.

Install (it is not published in the browser stores yet):

  • Chromium: download opentodo-browser-extension.zip from a release (or run make extension), unzip it, open chrome://extensions, turn on Developer mode, Load unpacked, pick the unzipped folder.
  • Firefox: open about:debugging#/runtime/this-firefox, Load Temporary Add-on…, pick manifest.json from the unzipped folder. Temporary add-ons are removed when Firefox restarts; a signed build is a release task.

First use: if no server is set, the extension opens its options page and asks for your server's address (for example https://todo.example.com). Once it is saved, the capture you started continues. Change it later in the extension's options.

Screenshot: right-click a page and choose Add screenshot to OpenTodo. The extension captures the visible part of the tab as a PNG and hands it to the capture popup, where it's listed under Files with the page's title and link; nothing is saved until you press Save. Handing the image to the popup needs access to your server's address, which the options page asks for when you save the address (you can also grant it later there). Without it the popup opens with the title and link and explains how to allow it.

Privacy: the extension stores only the server address (in the browser's extension sync storage). It holds no token or password, has no content scripts, and makes no network requests itself; the only traffic is the capture popup you open, which loads your own server. Permissions: activeTab (read the current tab's address, title and selection, and capture it, when you click), contextMenus, scripting (read the selection, and hand a screenshot to the popup), storage (the server address), and, optional, access to your server's address only, for the screenshot.

Signed out#

If the device is not signed in, the capture screen first shows the sign-in form with a note, then continues to the capture screen with the shared page intact. Until you save, the shared title, text and link stay in the page's memory only: they are removed from the address bar and are not written to storage or sent to the server (the server's request log records paths, never query strings). Reloading the sign-in page therefore loses the shared content; share it again.

Limits and safety#

  • The title is cut to 500 characters, the text to 16 KB with a [truncated] note.
  • A link is kept only if it starts with http:// or https://; anything else (javascript:, data:, file: …) is dropped and the rest of the share is shown normally.
  • Shared content is shown as plain text, never as HTML, and the capture screen never opens the shared link.
  • There is no auto-save: a link to /share cannot create a task without you pressing Save.
  • At most 10 files per share, none larger than the server's limit per file (25 MB unless the owner changed it); a larger file is listed as refused and the task is saved without it. On the public demo, files are not attached.
  • Shared files are listed by name, type and size and never shown as web pages; an HTML file is attached as a file that downloads.

pages.title: Import formats
pages.summary: Every import format in detail: your own export, CSV and other apps' JSON exports, mapping rules, duplicates and undo.
pages.html:
Import formats

OpenTodo imports tasks, projects, sections, recurrence rules and reminders from files: its own JSON export (for moving between instances or recovering), CSV from a spreadsheet or a script, and the JSON exports of other task managers. Open Settings → Data → Import data in the web app (or press g then Shift+I), or drive the same endpoints from a script; see API below.

Every import works in two steps:

  1. Preview. The server reads the file and reports, row by row, what would happen: create, update, skip (with a reason) or error (with the row number and the reason), with totals that also count new sections, recurring tasks and reminders, and file-level notes (for example comments that are not imported). Nothing is written.
  2. Import. The server runs the import as a background job. Every created or changed field becomes an ordinary operation in the op log, stamped with server time and the device id import, so every device receives the imported data on its next sync under the usual last-writer-wins rules. A whole import can be undone later.

Import runs on the server, so it needs a connection: the Import screen disables the file picker while offline and keeps showing the last loaded job list.

Formats#

The format is detected from the content, in this order; the preview shows what was detected and the format option overrides it.

Format id Recognised by Notes
opentodo a top-level "format": "opentodo-export" Exact round trip, see below
things-db a SQLite database with Things 3's tables a copy of Things' main.sqlite, see Things
json-items top-level items and projects arrays "projects / sections / items" backups
json-lists a top-level lists array lists of tasks; each list becomes a project
json-generic a top-level array of objects, or a tasks array a generic task list
todoist-csv a header starting with TYPE and containing CONTENT, PRIORITY, INDENT one project exported from Todoist, see Todoist
todoist-backup a ZIP of todoist-csv files Todoist's backup of every project
ticktick-csv a preamble starting with Date:, then a Folder Name, List Name, Title, Kind header TickTick's CSV backup, see TickTick
linear-csv a header with ID, Team, Title, Status, Priority and UUID Linear's workspace export, see Linear
csv a header row with a title column the documented columns below

ZIP files. A ZIP whose files are all of one format is imported as one job, one preview and one undo; each preview row shows the file it came from. Folders, __MACOSX/ and hidden files are skipped. An archive with more than 1,000 files, mixed formats, an unsafe file name, or more than ten times the upload limit when unpacked is refused with 400 invalid_file before anything is written. A zipped Things Database.thingsdatabase folder is read as a Things database.

A file matching none of these is refused with 400 unsupported_format, naming the supported formats. If a JSON export from another app is not recognised, convert it to the CSV columns below; every field the data model holds can be expressed there.

Own export (opentodo)#

The file from Settings → Data → Download export or GET /api/v1/export. Labels, projects (with their sub-project tree), sections, tasks (with subtasks, completion and tombstones), reminders and saved views are recreated with their original ids and field values, so importing an export into an empty account and exporting again gives an equivalent file (comments aside, see below).

Because ids are kept, nothing needs remapping: a task's section_id, a recurring series and its occurrence records (series_id, whose ids are derived from the series id), a reminder's task_id, a task's blocked_by and a dashboard's panels all point at the same entities as before. Every task field is carried: recurrence (stored in canonical form, for example Every Monday becomes every monday), series_id, section_id, notes_doc (rich-text notes), due including a zoned tz, estimate_minutes and ical_extra.

What is handled differently, and why:

  • Comments are not imported. A comment keeps its author, and the sync engine only accepts comments whose author_id is the account writing them; the authors in an export are accounts of the exporting instance (and other members of shared projects). Comment creation is also rate-limited per account. Rewriting every comment to you would misattribute other people's words, so the preview shows a note such as "12 comments are not imported" and nothing is written for them.
  • Assignees are kept only when they are you (a restore into the same account). Any other assignee_id names an account that is not a member here, so it is dropped with a warning on the task.
  • Reminders keep their delivered_at and dismissed_at, so a reminder that already went off stays quiet. A live reminder whose time has already passed and that was neither delivered nor dismissed for that time is imported dismissed at import time (with a warning), so restoring an old export does not push a burst of stale notifications. Future reminders fire normally. A reminder whose task is neither in the file nor in your account is an error row.
  • Attachments keep their ids, names and types and become yours: author_id is rewritten to you, comment_id is cleared (comments are not imported) and uploaded_at is set by the server once the file is stored. Links are always imported. A file needs the ZIP export (GET /api/v1/export?format=zip): the importer reads export.json and the files under attachments/<id>/<name>, checks each file against its size and sha256, and applies the server's per-file limit and your attachments total; a file that does not fit is left out and listed among the job's errors. From the JSON alone, file attachments are skipped and the preview says how many ("3 file attachments are not imported").
  • The read-only role and owner_id the export adds to shared projects are not data and are skipped silently; the end-to-end encryption key record is not imported.

When an id already exists in the account the row is skipped (exists), unless the existing option is overwrite: then only fields whose value differs are written (update), and fields that are unchanged keep their original clock, so a concurrent edit on a device is not clobbered needlessly. An entity that is deleted in the account is never resurrected (skip, reason deleted). Fields unknown to this server version are dropped with a warning.

Todoist (todoist-csv, todoist-backup)#

Todoist exports one project as CSV from the project's menu, and keeps backups of every project as a ZIP in its settings (Backups). The backup is the better choice: its file names carry the project names (Work [2203306141].csv), so projects keep their names. A single CSV does not name its project, so its tasks go to the target project.

Todoist Becomes
each file in the backup a project (the Inbox file goes to your Inbox or the target project)
meta row view_style=board the project opens as a board on the device that imports it
section row a section of the project
task row, INDENT 1, 2, 3 … a task; deeper indents are subtasks of the task above
PRIORITY 1–4 priority p1–p4 (1 is Todoist's red flag)
@label in CONTENT a label, removed from the title
DESCRIPTION the description
DATE with DATE_LANG the due date (and time); recurring dates become a rule, see below
DURATION in minutes the estimate
REMINDER_OFFSET / REMINDER_DATE a relative or absolute reminder
note row appended to the task's description under "Comments" (with a warning)
DEADLINE the task's deadline, read with DEADLINE_LANG like DATE; a value that cannot be read is kept as a "Deadline: …" line in the description (with a warning)
RESPONSIBLE dropped with a warning

DATE is the text Todoist showed, in the language named by DATE_LANG (English, German, French, Italian, Spanish or Portuguese): Oct 21, 21 Okt., 21 de octubre de 2027 15:00, tomorrow, every monday, jeden Montag, alle 2 Wochen. A date without a year takes the year of the export (the newest file time in the backup, otherwise the day you import). A recurring date becomes a rule whose first date is the next occurrence. A date that cannot be read leaves the task without a due date and adds a warning quoting it.

TickTick (ticktick-csv)#

TickTick's backup is one CSV, created from its settings (Backup). It starts with a few lines of metadata (the export date, the version and a status legend) before the header; the importer skips them.

TickTick Becomes
Folder Name a parent project
List Name a project inside its folder (Inbox goes to your Inbox or the target project)
View Mode kanban the project opens as a board on the importing device
Column Name the section
Kind CHECKLIST with item lines in Content a task with one subtask per item; checked items are completed
parentId the parent task
Tags labels
Content the description
Priority 5 / 3 / 1 / 0 p1 / p2 / p3 / p4
Due Date, Is All Day, Is Floating, Timezone the due date (and time) as you saw it in TickTick
Reminder reminders (for example -PT15M)
Repeat (RRULE) a recurrence rule, when the grammar can express it
Status 2 / -1 completed / completed with the label canceled (abandoned)

Linear (linear-csv)#

Linear exports a workspace's issues as CSV from its workspace settings (Import / Export).

Linear Becomes
Project (or Team when there is none) a project, which opens as a board on the importing device
Status a section, in the order statuses first appear, so the board shows the same columns
Title, Description the title, and the description starting with the issue identifier (ENG-123)
Priority Urgent / High / Medium / Low / No priority p1 / p2 / p3 / p4 / p4
Labels labels
Due Date the due date
Parent issue the parent task
Completed / Canceled completed / completed with the label canceled
Assignee kept when it is your own email address, otherwise dropped with a warning
Blocked by the issues it waits for become Blocked by, when they are in the same file; others are dropped with a warning
Estimate, cycles, milestones, initiatives, SLA, Related to, Duplicate of dropped with a warning

Things database (things-db)#

Things 3 has no export, but its database can be copied, as Cultured Code's support article "Accessing the Things database" explains. Quit Things first. On a Mac, open ~/Library/Group Containers/JLMPQHK86H.com.culturedcode.ThingsMac/, then the ThingsData-… folder, and copy Things Database.thingsdatabase. Upload its main.sqlite (right-click the folder and choose Show Package Contents), or a ZIP of the whole folder. On iPhone or iPad the article describes a diagnostics code that sends Things Database.aar; tap it to unpack it into the same folder.

The file is read from a private copy on the server, read-only, using only Things' own tables, and deleted after the preview or import. A SQLite file that is not a Things database is refused with 400 invalid_file.

Things Becomes
area a parent project
project a project inside its area
heading a section of its project
to-do a task in its project (or area, or your Inbox)
checklist item a subtask; checked items are completed
tag (nested tags as parent/child) a label
notes the description
start date ("When") the due date; a reminder time becomes a reminder
repeating to-do a recurrence rule, when the grammar can express it
completed / canceled completed / completed with the label canceled
deadline the task's deadline
Someday the task is parked (a Someday to-do that also has a date keeps the date, with a warning)
This Evening the task's evening flag
trashed items skipped

CSV (csv)#

UTF-8, with a header row. Comma, semicolon and tab separators are detected from the header; quote fields that contain the separator. Header names are case-insensitive and spaces or dashes count as underscores (Due Date is due_date). Only title is required.

Column Also accepted Value
title task, content, summary required
description notes, note text
project list, project_name project name; an existing project with the same name (ignoring case) is reused, otherwise one is created
section a section of the task's project (or a label, or ignored, by option); see Sections
parent parent_id the id of another row, or the title of exactly one row: the task becomes its subtask
id source_id your identifier for the row, used by parent and to recognise a repeated import
priority 1–4 or p1–p4 (1 highest); also high, medium, low, none; blank = 4
due_date due YYYY-MM-DD, YYYY-MM-DDTHH:MM[:SS] (floating) or with a Z/offset (converted to the chosen time zone)
due_time HH:MM; requires due_date
labels tags, label comma-separated label names; missing labels are created
completed_at a date, date-time or Unix time (milliseconds; seconds are recognised); true/yes/x/1 means "completed now"
completed done true/yes/x/1 marks the task completed at import time
created_at created like completed_at; defaults to the import time
recurrence repeat, repeats, recurring, rrule a recurrence rule, an RRULE or a common spelling; see Recurrence
reminder reminders one or more reminders separated by ;, , or |; see Reminders
start start_date someday parks the task, a date YYYY-MM-DD defers it until that day; with a due_date too, Someday is dropped with a warning
evening true/yes/x/1 marks the task for This Evening
deadline the day the task must be finished by, YYYY-MM-DD; a date-time keeps its date (with a warning); anything else is a row error
attachment attachments, files, links one or more http(s) addresses separated by ;, , or |, each kept as a link attachment; anything else is dropped with a warning
blocked_by depends_on, waits_for the rows this task waits for, by id or by a unique title, separated by ;, , or |; a row that is not in the file, or one that would make tasks wait for each other, is dropped with a warning

Columns named comment(s) or assignee are recognised as unsupported: a non-empty value is dropped with a warning on that row. Any other column is listed as ignored in the preview.

Rows are numbered like the file's lines (the header is row 1). A row with an invalid value is an error naming the row and the value, for example row 35: invalid priority "urgent!" (expected 1-4 or p1-p4).

id,title,project,section,parent,priority,due_date,due_time,labels,recurrence,reminder
1,Write report,Work,Q4,,p1,2026-10-20,14:30,"focus, deep",,30m before
2,Collect numbers,Work,Q4,1,2,2026-10-18,,,,
3,Water plants,,,,,,,home,every week,
4,Standup,Work,Daily,,,2026-10-13,09:30,,every weekday,15

json-generic#

A top-level array of task objects, or an object with a tasks array and an optional projects array ({id, name, parent_id}; parent_id makes sub-projects). Key names are matched leniently:

Task attribute Keys read
title title, name, content, summary, text
description description, notes, note, body
project project_id (an id from projects), or project / project_name / list (a name)
section section, section_name, column, heading
parent parent_id, parent, or nesting under subtasks / children
priority priority: 1–4, p1–p4, high/medium/low/none
due due, due_date, dueDate: a string, or {date, time?} / {datetime}
deadline deadline: a date string; a date-time keeps its date (with a warning)
labels labels, tags: strings, {name} objects or a comma-separated string
completion completed, done, checked (booleans), status: "completed", and completed_at / completedAt for the time
created created_at, createdAt, created
recurrence recurrence, rrule, repeat, recurring, recurrence_rule, recurrenceRule, repeatRule, or a due object with is_recurring and its string; a string, an array of RRULE strings or a {frequency, interval, days} object
reminders reminders, reminder, alarms, reminder_at, remind_at, reminderDateTime: one value or an array
attachments attachments, files, attachment: strings or {name, url} objects; http(s) addresses become link attachments, anything else is dropped with a warning

json-items#

An object with projects, sections, items and optionally labels, notes and reminders arrays joined by ids.

Source Becomes
projects[].name, parent_id project and sub-project; the source inbox (inbox_project: true) maps to the target project
items[].content, description title, description
items[].project_id, section_id project, section
sections[] sections of their project, created even when empty, in file order (with sections: section; deleted ones are skipped)
items[].parent_id subtask
items[].priority counted upwards in the source: 4 → 1, 3 → 2, 2 → 3, 1 → 4
items[].due.date due date (date-times with a zone are converted)
items[].due.is_recurring, due.string recurrence rule from the due string (every tue 4pm → every tuesday, every! 2 weeks → every 2 weeks after completion); a string that cannot be expressed is a warning
reminders[] (item_id) type: "relative" with minute_offset → reminder that many minutes before the due time; type: "absolute" with due.date → reminder at that time; location reminders and is_deleted ones are dropped (location with a warning)
items[].labels label names
items[].checked, completed_at, added_at completion, completion time, creation time
deadline ({date}) the task's deadline
notes[], duration dropped with a warning on the item

Items and projects marked is_deleted are skipped.

json-lists#

{"lists": [{"id", "title", "tasks": [...]}]}; each list becomes a project with its title. Tasks read title, notes (description), due (RFC 3339; converted to the chosen time zone), status: "completed" and completed (completion time), parent (a task id) or nested subtasks, and starred / important (priority 1). recurrence (string, RRULE array or {pattern: {type, interval, daysOfWeek}}) becomes a rule and reminderDateTime (or the other reminder keys of json-generic) a reminder. links are dropped with a warning; tasks marked deleted are skipped.

Mapping rules#

  • Projects are matched by name, ignoring case, against existing non-deleted projects; otherwise created. Tasks without a project go to the target project (option) or the Inbox.
  • Sections: see Sections.
  • Recurrence and reminders: see Recurrence and Reminders.
  • Subtasks are resolved after the whole file is read, so row order does not matter. A subtask joins its parent's project. A parent that is missing, invalid or would form a cycle leaves the task at the top level with a warning.
  • Labels are matched by name, ignoring case; missing ones are created.
  • Dates: plain dates stay dates; date-times without a zone keep their wall clock; date-times with a zone become the wall clock of that instant in the chosen time zone (default: the browser's zone in the web app, UTC through the API). Due dates are always stored floating. A deadline is a date only: a time on it is dropped with a warning, keeping the day as written. The preview counts the tasks that get a deadline.
  • Completion: a completed row keeps its source completion time, or the import time when the source has none.
  • Unsupported attributes (attachments that are not web addresses, comments, assignees, links, location reminders, recurrence rules the grammar cannot express) never block a row: the task is imported and the row carries a warning naming what was dropped.

Sections#

With sections: section (the default) a row's section becomes a real section of the task's project: an existing live section with the same name (ignoring case) is reused, otherwise one is created once per project, after the existing ones. A subtask's section is looked up in the project it ends up in. Tasks without a project (the Inbox, when no target project is chosen) cannot hold sections, so their section becomes a label, with a warning. sections: label turns every section into a label named like it (the behaviour before sections existed), sections: ignore drops them. Re-importing a file finds the sections it created by name (and, for json-items, by source id), so nothing is duplicated.

Recurrence#

A recurrence becomes a rule of the recurrence grammar, stored in canonical form, when the grammar can express it. Accepted, in this order:

  1. The grammar itself: every day, every 2 weeks, every monday, friday, every 15th, every last friday, every 3 days after completion, … until 2027-01-01, … for 10 times.
  2. An iCalendar RRULE, with or without the RRULE: prefix (FREQ=WEEKLY;INTERVAL=2, FREQ=MONTHLY;BYDAY=-1FR), when it maps exactly onto a rule (as for CalDAV).
  3. Common spellings: daily, weekly, monthly, yearly, annually, biweekly, fortnightly, every other day|week|month|year, weekdays, every workday, every weekend, each … and ev … for every …, and every! … for "after completion" (every! 3 days → every 3 days after completion). A trailing time of day (every tue 4pm, every day at 09:00) is removed: the due time carries it.
  4. A structured object {frequency|freq|type|unit, interval, days|daysOfWeek|byday} (also under pattern), e.g. {"frequency": "weekly", "days": ["MO", "TH"]} → every monday, thursday, and an array of RRULE strings.

Anything else (hourly rules, starting …, every other monday, an interval combined with weekdays, free text) is shown in the preview as a warning on the row, recurrence "every 3 hours" not supported; imported without a rule, and the task is imported without a rule. A recurring task without a due date gets the rule's first date from today in the chosen time zone, as in the app. Imported recurring tasks are series of their own (no series_id).

Reminders#

Reminders are created together with their task (a task that is skipped, for example as already imported, brings none) and belong to you, like every reminder.

Value Becomes
a number, or a string of digits relative reminder that many minutes before the due time
30m, 1h, 2 days, 15 min before relative reminder before the due time
an ISO 8601 duration (-PT15M, -P1D) relative reminder; a negative duration is before the due time
a date-time (2026-10-20T08:00, with or without zone) or a date absolute reminder at that time (floating values in the chosen time zone, a date at 09:00)
an object with offset_minutes (negative = before), minute_offset / minutes_before (minutes before) or offset / trigger (a duration) relative reminder
an object with datetime, at, remind_at, fire_at, time, date or due.date absolute reminder
type: "location" dropped with a warning

A relative reminder fires at the due time plus its offset, with a date-only due counting as 09:00, in the chosen time zone. On a task without a due date it is kept but does not fire (the row says so). A reminder whose time has already passed at import time is imported dismissed, with a warning, so no stale notification is sent. Offsets beyond one year are dropped with a warning.

Duplicates#

Checked in this order:

  1. Own export: an id that already exists is skip (exists) or, with existing: overwrite, update.
  2. A source row recorded by an earlier, not undone import of the same format for this account is skip (already_imported). Importing the same file twice therefore creates nothing the second time. CSV rows without an id column are recognised by their content.
  3. A row whose title (trimmed, ignoring case), project and due date match an existing open task is skip (possible_duplicate), unless the duplicates option is import, in which case it is created with a warning.

Options#

Option Values Default
format a format id from the table above detected
targetProject id of one of your projects Inbox
timeZone IANA zone, e.g. Europe/Rome UTC (the web app sends the browser zone)
sections section, label, ignore section
duplicates skip, import skip
errors skip_rows, abort skip_rows
existing skip, overwrite (own export only) skip

With skip_rows, bad rows are reported and everything else is imported; a bad row never leaves a partial task. With abort, any row in error fails the job before anything is written and names the first bad row.

Jobs, limits and undo#

  • One import job per account runs at a time; starting a second one answers 409 conflict naming the running job.
  • Files may be at most OPENTODO_IMPORT_MAX_MB megabytes (default 20, allowed 1–200) and 50,000 rows; larger files answer 413 too_large.
  • Ops are written in batches of at most 1,000 and progress is saved after each batch. If the server restarts mid-import, the job shows failed with the counts of what was written, and undo removes it.
  • Undo tombstones every project, task, label, section, reminder and saved view the job created, through the op log: they disappear from every view and from other devices after their next sync, and stay in the export with deleted_at. Entities the job only updated are left alone. As when deleting in the app, open tasks you later added to an undone project move to the Inbox, open tasks you later put into an undone section move to "No section", and undone labels are removed from your other tasks. Undo is idempotent. After an undo the same file can be imported again.
  • Webhooks see an import as one import.completed delivery per finished job and one import.undone per undo, not one event per task. See Webhooks → Imports.

Job records (status, options, counts, row errors) are operational metadata kept in the server database; they are not part of the export.

Memory#

The preview reads the whole file once. CSV is streamed record by record; a JSON file is decoded in one piece and takes roughly five times its size in memory, so the largest default file (20 MB of JSON) peaks around 100–120 MB during the preview and the start of the job, released afterwards. Typical imports of a few thousand rows stay under 10 MB. On a 1 GB Raspberry Pi keep the default or lower OPENTODO_IMPORT_MAX_MB.

API#

All routes require a session or a bearer token, like the rest of the API. Uploads are multipart/form-data with a file part and the options either as one JSON options part or as individual fields named like the options.

# Preview (nothing is written)
curl -sS "$OT/api/v1/import/preview" -H "Authorization: Bearer $TOKEN" \
  -F file=@tasks.csv -F timeZone=Europe/Rome

# Start the job → 202 {"job": {"id": "…", "status": "running", …}}
curl -sS "$OT/api/v1/import" -H "Authorization: Bearer $TOKEN" \
  -F file=@opentodo-export.json -F 'options={"existing":"overwrite"}'

# Follow it, list jobs, undo
curl -sS "$OT/api/v1/import/jobs/<id>" -H "Authorization: Bearer $TOKEN"
curl -sS "$OT/api/v1/import/jobs" -H "Authorization: Bearer $TOKEN"
curl -sS -X POST "$OT/api/v1/import/jobs/<id>/undo" -H "Authorization: Bearer $TOKEN"

See docs/api.md for the response shapes and error codes.

pages.html:
End-to-end encryption

Optional, per account, off by default (OpenSpec change e2ee). When it is on, your devices encrypt the content of your tasks before it is synced, so the server, its backups and every server-side integration hold only ciphertext for it. Sync, offline use and conflict-free merging keep working because ciphertext travels through the unchanged operation log as an ordinary string value.

Turn it on in Settings → Encryption.

What is encrypted, what is not#

Encrypted, in your personal data (Inbox, your own projects, labels, saved views):

Entity Encrypted fields
task title, description, ical_extra, notes_doc (the rich-text note document, encrypted as one opaque string; its ciphertext must fit the 256 KB document limit, so an encrypted note document is capped at about 196 KB)
project name
label name
section name
saved view name, query
comment body (your comments on your own tasks)
attachment name, mime (the file type), url (a link's address), and the file itself, as an encrypted file (see below)

Everything else stays plaintext, because views sort and group by it, reminders and calendars schedule with it, and the server needs it to merge and authorize: due (date, time, zone), priority, completed_at, deleted_at, created_at, position, project_id, parent_id, section_id, labels (the list of label ids on a task), recurrence, estimate_minutes, assignee_id, project color and archived, reminder times, an attachment's size and sha256 (of the encrypted file) and encrypted flag, and all timestamps and device ids of operations.

Empty values ("") and null are not encrypted. The length of a ciphertext reveals the approximate length of the text.

Shared projects are never encrypted. A project that was shared before you enabled encryption, and projects other people share with you, stay plaintext for every member. While encryption is on you cannot share a project that is not shared yet (409 encryption_enabled): the members would hold no key.

Threat model#

Protected against:

  • Someone who reads the server's disk, database file, backups (local, S3, WebDAV) or database dumps: they see ciphertext for the fields above.
  • The server operator browsing the data, and server-side integrations (CalDAV, the MCP endpoint, webhooks, the REST API with an API token): they see ciphertext or a placeholder.
  • A server or a bug moving a ciphertext to another field or task: the value is bound to entity, entityId and field and fails authentication; the app shows "[Cannot decrypt]" and keeps the operation.

Not protected against (honest limits):

  • Metadata. Everything in the plaintext list above, plus how many tasks, projects and labels you have, when you edit what, from how many devices, and the approximate length of each text.
  • A malicious or compromised server serving tampered JavaScript. The web app is delivered by the same server it protects you from. A server that changes the code can capture the passphrase or the key on the next load. This is inherent to web-delivered end-to-end encryption; a future change may verify release signatures in the service worker.
  • Your devices. The device is the trust boundary: local storage (IndexedDB) holds plaintext and the account key (as a non-extractable CryptoKey). Malware, a browser extension with access to the page, or someone with your unlocked device can read everything. "Lock this device" forgets the key and pauses sync but leaves already synced data in local storage; Sign out clears local data.
  • Weak passphrases. The server holds the passphrase-wrapped key. Someone with that record can try passphrases offline; PBKDF2 with 600,000 iterations slows this down but is not memory-hard. Use a long passphrase (at least 12 characters are required).
  • Plaintext that existed before. Content written before encryption was enabled, or written in plaintext later (REST, email), stays in older backups and in the server's history until you purge it (see below).
  • Your account itself. Encryption protects content, not access: anyone who can sign in can delete, reschedule or tombstone your (encrypted) tasks, and can read the plaintext fields.

How it works#

Key hierarchy, all generated and used in the browser with the built-in Web Crypto API (no dependency):

  • Account key: 256 random bits, AES-256-GCM. Kept on each unlocked device as a non-extractable key in IndexedDB.
  • Passphrase key: PBKDF2-HMAC-SHA-256 over your passphrase (NFC-normalised) with a 16-byte random salt and 600,000 iterations, producing an AES-KW key.
  • Recovery key: 256 random bits, shown once as 56 base32 characters in 14 groups of four (52 for the key, 4 for a checksum). HKDF-SHA-256 (fixed salt, info opentodo/e2ee/recovery-kek/v1) turns it into an AES-KW key.
  • The account key is wrapped (AES-KW, RFC 3394) under both. The key record — {version, kdf, salt, iterations, wrappedByPassphrase, wrappedByRecovery} — is the only key material the server stores (encryption_keys table). It never receives the passphrase, the recovery key or the account key.

Value format (a string in the existing op value):

"enc:v1:" + base64url( nonce(12 bytes) || AES-256-GCM(utf8(plaintext)) || tag(16 bytes) )
additional authenticated data = utf8(entity + "\0" + entityId + "\0" + field)

Nonces are 96 random bits per encryption. Known-answer vectors shared by the Go and browser test suites are in web/src/lib/e2ee.vectors.json.

Attached files are encrypted on the device in 1 MiB chunks, so a large file is never held in memory twice:

header  = "OTAT1" || chunk size (4 bytes, big-endian) || file prefix (8 random bytes)
chunk i = AES-256-GCM(chunk i of the file) || tag(16 bytes)
nonce i = file prefix || i (3 bytes, big-endian) || 0x01 on the last chunk, else 0x00
additional authenticated data = utf8("attachment\0" + attachment id + "\0") || header

The id in every chunk binds the bytes to their attachment, and the marked last chunk means a cut-off file is detected. The server stores and serves the encrypted file as opaque bytes (always as a download), and its size and sha256 describe the encrypted file, never the original. Opening a file downloads it to the device, checks and decrypts every chunk, and only then shows it: a chunk that fails the check means nothing is shown. An encrypted file is about 16 bytes per MiB larger than the original, so a file just under the per-file limit can be refused once encrypted. Thumbnails are not shown for encrypted images.

Where it happens on the device:

  • Every edit is applied locally in plaintext and queued. The sync engine encrypts content fields at the single point where operations leave the device (just before upload), so nothing reaches the server in plaintext whichever path created the operation (edits, re-seeding after a server restore, the migration, encrypt-on-sight).
  • Incoming operations are decrypted before they are applied, so search, filters and views work on plaintext locally.
  • Convergence is unchanged: winners are chosen by (timestamp, device), never by value. Two ciphertexts of the same text differ, which does not matter.

Content larger than 48,000 bytes (UTF-8) in one field is refused before an operation is created, because its ciphertext would exceed the server's 64 KiB value limit.

Devices, locking and offline use#

  • New device: sign in, then enter the passphrase (or the recovery key) on the unlock screen. Nothing is pulled or pushed before that; the sync status reads Locked. Afterwards the device works offline and does not ask again.
  • Wrong passphrase: an error, and after 5 failures within a minute further attempts are delayed for the rest of that minute (on this device).
  • Lock this device (Settings): forgets the key and pauses sync until unlocked.
  • Offline unlock works once the device has seen the key record.
  • A device that did not know encryption had been enabled notices the first ciphertext it receives, checks the key record and locks itself without applying the batch.

Passphrase change, recovery, losing both#

  • Change passphrase (needs the current one and a fresh sign-in confirmation): re-wraps the account key; content is not re-encrypted; other devices keep working; new devices use the new passphrase.
  • Reset with the recovery key (forgotten passphrase): sets a new passphrase and issues a new recovery key; the old one stops working.
  • Lost both: the content cannot be recovered by anyone, including the server owner — there is no server-side reset. Settings and the unlock screen offer only to turn encryption off and delete the encrypted content: the key record is removed and every item whose content cannot be decrypted is moved to the Trash as it syncs. Plaintext fields (dates, structure) are kept.

Enabling, plaintext that appears later, purging, disabling#

  • Enabling re-writes every content field of your personal data as ciphertext through ordinary operations, with progress in Settings; the job is resumable after a reload. 500 tasks produce roughly 1,500 operations. Then each attached file is downloaded, encrypted and uploaded again as a new attachment that replaces the plaintext one ("Encrypting your files: 3 of 40 files"). This part needs a connection: it stops when the network goes and continues after the next sync, and files not done yet keep their old form meanwhile.
  • Plaintext written later — through the REST API, the CLI, email-to-task or an import — is accepted by the server and shown with a small "not yet encrypted" marker; the next unlocked device that syncs it re-writes it as ciphertext ("encrypt-on-sight"). Two devices doing that at once produce two ciphertexts of the same text; one wins and nothing is re-written again.
  • Purge plaintext history (POST /api/v1/encryption/purge-history) deletes the superseded operations of the content fields in your personal data, including the plaintext from before encryption. Winners stay, so every device still converges. The deletion runs with SQLite secure_delete, then the database is vacuumed and the write-ahead log truncated. Revision history for those fields is gone afterwards. Backups made before the purge, and copies of the database, may still contain plaintext: delete them if that matters to you.
  • Disabling (needs an unlocked device and a fresh sign-in confirmation) first re-uploads every encrypted file decrypted, while encryption is still on, and waits until the last one is stored on the server, so no file becomes unreadable. Then it deletes the key record, so other devices stop encrypting, and re-writes all content as plaintext. Devices that still hold the key decrypt ciphertext that arrives late and re-write it as plaintext too.

Server-side reads and integrations#

The server cannot decrypt. Each feature that needs content degrades explicitly:

Feature Behaviour for an encrypted account
REST API reads Return the ciphertext string in content fields, plaintext elsewhere. Scripts need the key to decrypt (format above).
REST API writes Accepted in plaintext; encrypted on sight by the next unlocked device.
Export (GET /api/v1/export) Ciphertext content, plaintext scheduling fields, and the wrapped key record under encryption, enough to decrypt elsewhere with the passphrase. Importing it into another account keeps the ids (so the binding still matches), but that account needs the same key record to decrypt.
Import Writes plaintext like REST; duplicate detection by name/title cannot match encrypted labels and projects, so an import may create duplicates.
Backups Hold ciphertext and the wrapped key record (plus any plaintext not yet purged).
CalDAV Refused: /dav/ answers 403 for the account and creating an app password answers 409 encryption_enabled. Calendar clients can neither read ciphertext nor write it back, and placeholders would overwrite real titles.
MCP (assistants) Encrypted titles, descriptions, project, label and section names read as "Encrypted item" with "encrypted": true; search_tasks never matches them. Dates, priorities and structure are still reported. Write tools that need readable text are not offered and are refused with encryption_enabled; scheduling, completing, moving, priorities and labels still work.
Email to task Creates plaintext Inbox tasks (the mail crossed mail servers in the clear anyway); encrypted on sight; purge removes the plaintext operations.
Webhooks Payloads carry the stored value: ciphertext for encrypted fields.
Reminder pushes An encrypted title is never put in the push payload, even for devices that opted in to content; the notification shows the content-free text.
Notifications (assignment, mention) Use "Encrypted item" instead of a ciphertext title (only relevant if ciphertext ever reaches a shared project).
Revision history, activity Served as stored; the web app decrypts values for display.
Sharing First share of a project refused with 409 encryption_enabled.
Filters Evaluated on the device on plaintext; nothing server-side.

API#

See api.md: GET/PUT/DELETE /api/v1/encryption/keys, POST /api/v1/encryption/purge-history, encryption and minClientVersion in GET /api/v1/me and GET /api/v1/auth/status.

s: This guide takes you from opening OpenTodo for the first time to adding a task, giving it a date and ticking it off. It takes about five minutes. You can follow along in the demo or on your own server.

Go to demo.open-todo.app and select Try the demo. You get a private sandbox filled with sample projects and tasks. Nobody else can see it, and it is deleted after two hours without activity (and every night), so don't keep anything personal there.

The first person to open a new OpenTodo server creates the owner account. Enter your name, email and a password of at least 10 characters, then select Create owner account. After that, sign-up is closed: other people join with an invitation from you (see Sharing and comments).

Open the invitation link you were sent, choose a name and password, and you're in. If your server offers single sign-on or passkeys, the sign-in screen shows those buttons too. Once you're signed in, the app is stored on your device. You can keep using it without a connection, and it catches up with the server when you're back online.

The sidebar on the left lists your views and projects. On a phone it's behind the menu button at the top left. Inbox collects tasks that don't belong to a project yet. Today shows what's due today, with anything overdue at the top. Upcoming shows the days ahead, grouped by date. Projects are your own lists, like "Home renovation" or "Work". The circle to the left of each task completes it. The small line under the title shows the date, labels and project. More on all the views in Views.

Press q, or click the Add a task box at the top of the list. Type what you need to do, for example Call the dentist. Press Enter. The task appears straight away. The box stays open, so you can type the next one right after. Where the task goes depends on where you are: in a project it goes into that project, in Today it's due today, and in the Inbox it waits there until you sort it.

You can schedule a task while you type it. Quick add understands everyday words: Call the dentist tomorrow at 9am As you type, small chips appear under the box to show what OpenTodo understood: a date chip for "tomorrow at 9am", and below them the title that will be saved. If a word was picked up by mistake ("May" as in the name, not the month), click the × on its chip and it stays part of the title. The same line can also set a project with #, a label with @, a priority from p1 (highest) to p4, and how long it will take with +, like +15m. The quick add reference lists everything it understands, in six languages. To change the date later, open the task (click it, or select it and press Enter) and use Due in the panel that opens.

When you're done, click the circle next to the task, or select it with j and k and press c. The task leaves the list and moves to Completed in the sidebar. Changed your mind? Open Completed and reopen it.
OpenTodo runs in the browser, and you can install it like an app on your phone, tablet or computer. It then opens in its own window and works offline. See Installing the app.

Every guide on this site is also in the app: select Help at the bottom of the sidebar, or press g then ?. It works offline and matches the version of your server. Many screens have a small Help link that opens the right section next to what you're doing, without closing it.

Tasks and projects: notes, subtasks, priorities and organising your work. Views: Today, Upcoming, the calendar and views you save yourself. Recurring tasks and reminders: repeat a task every week and get a nudge on time. Keyboard shortcuts: press ? in the app to see them all.

OpenTodo is a web app you can install. Once installed it has its own icon, opens in its own window without browser bars, starts without a connection, and on most platforms can show reminders while it's closed. There is no app store involved: you install it from your server's address, and updates arrive by themselves. Before you start, open your OpenTodo address in the browser and sign in once. Installing needs a secure address (one starting with https://); if your browser offers no install option at all, ask whoever runs your server to set that up.

Open your OpenTodo address in Safari. Tap the Share button (the square with an arrow pointing up). Scroll down and tap Add to Home Screen, then Add. OpenTodo now has an icon on your home screen. Open it from there from now on. On iOS 16.4 and later, push notifications for reminders work only in the installed app, not in a Safari tab; turn them on in Settings → Notifications inside the app. See Notifications. Recent iOS versions also offer Add to Home Screen from the share menu of other browsers. If you don't see it, use Safari.

Open your OpenTodo address in Chrome (Edge and Samsung Internet work the same way). Open the browser menu (⋮). Tap Install app. On some versions it's called Add to Home screen. Chrome sometimes shows an install banner at the bottom of the screen on its own; tapping it does the same thing. After installing, OpenTodo also appears in Android's share menu, so you can send a link or some text from another app straight into a new task. See Capturing pages.

In Chrome or Edge: Open your OpenTodo address. Click the install icon at the right end of the address bar (a small screen with a down arrow), or open the browser menu and choose Install OpenTodo (in Edge: Apps → Install this site as an app). Confirm with Install. OpenTodo opens in its own window and gets an entry in your Start menu, Dock or app launcher. You can pin it to the taskbar like any other app. In Safari on macOS (Sonoma or later), choose File → Add to Dock. Firefox on the desktop doesn't install web apps. You can still use OpenTodo in a Firefox tab with everything working, including offline use once the page has loaded.

The installed app keeps a full copy of your tasks on the device. You can open it on a plane, add and complete tasks, and it syncs when you're online again. The status at the top right tells you where things stand. More in Offline and sync.

When your server is updated, the app fetches the new version in the background and switches to it on its own, usually with one quick reload. If you think you're still on an old version, close the app completely and open it again.

Remove it the way you remove any app on that device: long-press the icon and choose Remove App (iPhone) or Uninstall (Android), or use Uninstall from the app window's menu on a computer. Your tasks stay on your server. Signing out (Settings → Account → Sign out of this device) clears the copy of your tasks on that device. Changes that haven't reached the server yet are uploaded first when you're online.
Your projects, sections, subtasks, labels, priorities, due dates and recurring tasks come with you. It takes a few minutes, and you can undo the whole import with one click.

Use a backup: it holds every project and keeps their names. In Todoist, open its settings and find Backups. Download the latest backup. It is a ZIP file such as Todoist_backup_2026-09-19.zip. A single project can also be exported as CSV from the project's menu, but a lone CSV file does not say which project it was, so its tasks go to the project you choose when importing.

Open Settings → Data → Import data (or press g then Shift+I). Choose the ZIP file. The preview shows Todoist backup (ZIP) and lists every project, section and task. Check the warnings, choose a time zone if your tasks have times, and select Import. Projects that were boards in Todoist open as boards on this device. Your other devices receive everything on their next sync.

Projects, sections and subtasks (by their indent), in the same order. Priorities: Todoist's red flag is p1, as you saw it. Labels written in tasks (@errands), removed from the title. Descriptions and estimates (task durations in minutes). Due dates and times, in the language you used Todoist in (English, German, French, Italian, Spanish or Portuguese). Dates without a year take the year of the backup. Recurring dates such as every monday or jeden Montag, when OpenTodo's recurrence rules can express them. Reminders with a time or an offset. The full mapping is in Import formats.

Comments are added to the task's description under "Comments", because their authors cannot be kept. Deadlines are kept as a "Deadline: …" line in the description; OpenTodo has no deadline field yet. Assignees are dropped; invite people and share the project instead. Dates or rules OpenTodo cannot read leave the task without a due date, with a warning that quotes them. Changed your mind? Undo the import from the list of past imports.
Things 3 has no export button, but OpenTodo can read a copy of its database directly. Your areas, projects, headings, to-dos, checklists, tags and notes come with you.

On a Mac, as Cultured Code's support article "Accessing the Things database" describes: Quit Things. The copy must be made while the app is closed. In Finder, choose Go → Go to Folder and open ~/Library/Group Containers/JLMPQHK86H.com.culturedcode.ThingsMac/. Open the ThingsData-… folder and copy (do not move) Things Database.thingsdatabase to your Desktop. Right-click the copy, choose Show Package Contents, and find main.sqlite. Alternatively, compress the whole folder into a ZIP. On iPhone or iPad, the same article lists a diagnostics code (Settings → General → Diagnostics → Enter Code) that sends Things Database.aar. Save it to Files, tap it to unpack it into Things Database.thingsdatabase, and use the main.sqlite inside.

Open Settings → Data → Import data (or press g then Shift+I). Choose main.sqlite (or the ZIP). The preview shows Things 3 database. Check the warnings and select Import. The file is read on your server from a private copy, read-only, and deleted right after the preview or import.

Areas become parent projects; projects stay inside them. Headings become sections; to-dos keep their heading. Checklist items become subtasks, completed ones included. Tags become labels (nested tags as parent/child). Notes, the start date ("When") as the due date, and reminder times. Repeating to-dos, when OpenTodo's recurrence rules can express them. Completed and canceled items (canceled ones get the label canceled). The full mapping is in Import formats.
Deadlines are kept as a "Deadline: …" line in the description. Someday and This Evening are not imported as such; the to-dos arrive with a warning. Trashed items are skipped.
Your folders, lists, board columns, checklists, tags, priorities, due dates, reminders and repeating tasks come with you.
TickTick creates a backup as one CSV file from its settings (look for Backup). Download it; it is named like TickTick-backup-2026-10-14.csv.

Open Settings → Data → Import data (or press g then Shift+I). Choose the CSV file. The preview shows TickTick backup (CSV). Check the warnings and select Import. Lists you used as a board (kanban) open as boards on this device.

Folders become parent projects; lists become projects inside them. Board columns become sections. Checklists become a task with one subtask per item; checked items are completed. Subtasks, tags, descriptions and priorities (high, medium, low, none become p1–p4). Due dates and times as you saw them, all-day tasks as dates. Reminders and repeat rules, when OpenTodo's recurrence rules can express them. Completed tasks; abandoned ones are completed with the label canceled. The full mapping is in Import formats.
Attachments, habits, focus records and comments are not part of the CSV backup. Repeat rules OpenTodo cannot express are dropped with a warning; the task is kept.
OpenTodo is a good fit for small teams and personal work that want speed without process. Your issues come with their projects, statuses, priorities, labels, due dates and sub-issues.
Linear exports a workspace's issues as one CSV file from its workspace settings (look for Import / Export).

Open Settings → Data → Import data (or press g then Shift+I). Choose the CSV file. The preview shows Linear export (CSV). Check the warnings and select Import. Each project opens as a board on this device, with one column per status.

Projects (or teams, for issues without a project). Statuses become sections, in the order they appear, so the board shows the same columns. Titles, and descriptions that start with the issue identifier (ENG-123), so you can still find it. Priorities (Urgent, High, Medium, Low and No priority become p1–p4), labels and due dates. Sub-issues as subtasks. Completed issues; canceled ones are completed with the label canceled. Issues assigned to you stay assigned to you. The full mapping is in Import formats.

Blocked by relations between issues in the export become Blocked by on the tasks. Estimates (points), cycles, milestones, initiatives, SLAs and the other issue relations (related, duplicate) are dropped with a warning. Issues assigned to other people arrive unassigned; share the project and assign them again. Comments and attachments are not part of the CSV export.
A task is one thing to do. A project is a list of tasks that belong together. This guide covers both, from adding a task to arranging projects inside each other.

Press q anywhere in a task list, type, and press Enter. The box stays focused so you can add several in a row. You can fill in details as you type: Order new taps friday #Home @errand p2 +20m This creates "Order new taps", due Friday, in the project Home, with the label errand, priority 2 and an estimate of 20 minutes. Chips under the box show what was understood before you press Enter. The quick add reference has every word and symbol it knows. New tasks without a project land in the Inbox. Tasks added inside a project go into that project, and tasks added in Today are due today.

Click a task, or select it with j / k and press Enter, to open its panel. Every change is saved as you make it; there is no Save button. The top of the panel has Complete, a ⋯ menu with Copy link, Open parent task, Open recurring task and Delete, and the × that closes it. Below are the Title and Notes. Notes can have headings, bold and italic text, links, and bullet, numbered and check lists. Then comes the properties card. Each row shows its current value, or a quiet "No due date", "No estimate" and so on when it is empty. Click a row, or Tab to it and press Enter, to change it; Esc closes the editor and leaves you on the row. Project, Section and Parent task move the task. Each opens a list you can search: the projects and tasks you pick most often come first, and nested projects show their path ("Work › Clients"), so two projects with the same name are told apart. Type a new name in Project and choose Create to make a project and move the task into it. A subtask always shows its parent's section. Assignee. See Assign tasks. Priority, from P1 (most important) to P4 (the default). Click one, or press 1 to 4 anywhere in the panel outside a text field. Due, a date with an optional time, and the time zone chip next to it. When (Anytime, a start date or Someday) and Evening. See When a task starts. Deadline, the day the task must be finished by, with how many days are left. Type it like a due date (fri, 2026-11-06) or clear it with ×. See Deadlines. Reminders show as chips. Add

You don't have to open a task to change it. Select it and press: Key Does 1 to 4 Set the priority c Complete or reopen L Add labels (type to search, Enter to add or create) e Set the estimate (20, 45m, 1h30) d Set the deadline (fri, 2026-11-06) n Park in Someday, or bring back Shift+N Defer: type the start date Shift+E Toggle This Evening x Tick for a bulk action (see Change several tasks at once) s Schedule it on the Day calendar Delete Move it to the Trash

The notes field formats as you type. Start a line with - for a bullet list, 1. for a numbered list, [ ] for a checklist or # for a heading. Select text and press Ctrl+B for bold or Ctrl+K for a link (⌘ on a Mac). If two of your devices edit the same note at the same time, both sets of changes are kept.

A due date is just a calendar day, and a time is the time on the clock where you are. A task due Tuesday at 09:00 shows Tuesday at 09:00 on every device, even when you travel. Type the date and time in the Due fields, or pick them. Dates and times are shown in the format you chose in Settings → Preferences → Date and time, and you can type them the same way: Date: a date in your format (14/10 or 10/14, with or without a year), an ISO date (2026-10-14), or a word: today, tomorrow, a weekday such as fri, next week or 3 Nov. A date without a year that has already passed this year means next year. Press Enter or leave the field to save it. If the date doesn't exist (31/02), the field says so and the task keeps its date. Calendar: the calendar button next to the date, or Alt+↓ in the field, opens a month whose weeks start on your first day of the week. Arrow keys move by day and week, Page Up and Page Down by month, Home and End to the start and end of the week, Enter picks the day and Esc closes it. Time: 15, 1530, 15:30, 3pm, 3:30 pm or noon, whichever clock you use. ↓ in the field shows times in 15-minute steps to pick from. Clear the date to remove the due date, or clear the time to keep only the day. Under the due date, the time zone button shows how the time is meant: Floating (the same clock time wherever you are) or a city and its offset, such as New York · UTC−5 (one moment worldwide). Choose it to: Fix to my zone: tie the time to your current time zone, for things that h

The due date is when you plan to work on a task. A deadline is the day it must be finished by, and the two are separate: you can plan a report for Tuesday that is due to your boss on Friday. Moving or clearing the due date never changes the deadline, and you may even plan a task after its deadline; the countdown then turns red. A task with a deadline shows a countdown on its row, next to an hourglass: 3d for three days to go, Today on the day, and 2d over once it has passed. It turns amber in the last week and red on the day and after. Hover it to see the full date. The countdown follows the calendar on your device, so it moves on at midnight even offline. Deadlines also bring tasks into Today and Upcoming, and you can add a reminder before the deadline (see Reminders).

Not every task is for now. The When row in the panel says when a task becomes relevant: Anytime, the default: the task is in your lists as usual. A start date defers the task until that day: it disappears from Today, Upcoming, Anytime and the counts, and its project or Inbox lists it at the end under Later, with a Starts 21 Oct chip. On its start day it appears in Today with a Started chip and stays there until you deal with it. The start date can't be after the due date. Someday parks the task: it moves to the Someday view and its project's Later group, and its due date is cleared (a repeating task stops repeating). Giving it a due date or a start date brings it back. A due date or a deadline that has come always shows the task in Today, even if it is deferred or parked. This Evening (the Evening switch next to it) moves a task due today into its own group below the day's tasks in Today, and shows a moon on its row elsewhere. It says nothing about the time of day. From the list: n parks a task or brings it back, Shift+N asks for its start date, and Shift+E toggles This Evening.

Some tasks can't start until another is done: you can't book flights before the dates are confirmed. Open the task, choose Blocked by (or select it in a list and press b) and pick the tasks it waits for. The list offers open tasks you can link: the task itself, tasks that already wait for it and tasks shared differently are left out, so you can't make two tasks wait for each other. While at least one of those tasks is open, the task is blocked: its row is dimmed and shows a lock with the number it's waiting for, on boards too, and in Today it moves to a folded Blocked group at the end. As soon as the last one is completed (or deleted), the task is ready again, on every device. You can still open, edit and complete a blocked task; completing it doesn't touch the tasks it waited for. A repeating task keeps blocking until its series ends, and Blocked by says "repeats" next to it. Blocks in the panel lists the open tasks waiting for this one; select one to open it. In a shared project, blockers are tasks of the same project, and the person a blocked task is assigned to gets a notification when it's ready to start.
